About this document

This is the user manual for Proxalume (Software Intelligence Workbench, by WildCat Studio). It works offline and needs no installation. Use the search box above to find a topic.

Online documentation. This complete manual is a snapshot of the 2.0.8 development documentation. Screenshots may show earlier interface layouts or branding. Consult the official product site and the guide bundled with your installed version for current release availability, licensing terms and version-specific behavior.

Download the complete offline HTML manual · Official Proxalume site · Project showcase

How it is organized

  • Overview and Quick start: what the product does, how licensing and the 14-day trial work, and how to begin.
  • User Guide: every topic of the guide that is built into the application under Help > Documentation.
  • Settings and Limitations: what you can configure and what the application does not do.

Product overview

Proxalume is a local-first desktop workbench that turns unfamiliar software and incident artifacts into structured evidence you can explore on your own computer:

  • Source-code analysis. Open a project folder or clone a Git repository and explore it as a 2D graph, a 3D code city, route flow, database schema, security findings, supply-chain inventory, project health and change impact.
  • Binary Workbench. Open a compiled program, archive, installer, firmware image or Windows minidump without running it, and inspect its hashes, entropy, strings, imports, functions, control-flow graphs, native pseudo-code and cross-references. Add annotations, synchronize shared notes, compare two versions and patch with undo.
  • Forensic Case Management. Preserve suspect files with simultaneous SHA-256, SHA-1 and MD5 digests, maintain an immutable chain-of-custody ledger, triage Windows shortcuts (.lnk), Prefetch execution traces (.pf), browser SQLite histories and minidump memory anomalies, and export encrypted .proxcase bundles.

Privacy and safety

  • Analysis is offline and local by default. Your code, binaries and forensic evidence are read, not run, and no project or sample data is sent anywhere.
  • Repositories, archives and binaries you open are treated as untrusted: nothing in them executes during static analysis or forensic triage. The one interactive exception is the debugger (Binary > Debug Open Binary (runs it)…), which runs the open program only after you confirm its SHA-256 hash.
  • Online license activation and signed update checks contact the publisher's HTTPS service only when you invoke them and never transmit file names, paths or code.
  • The optional AI assistant is off by default and talks only to a service you configure. If you choose a cloud service, only the code, findings or summaries you ask it about are sent to that service.

Quick start

Starting the application

Unzip the package and run Proxalume.exe (Windows) or ./Proxalume (Linux; if permissions were not preserved, run chmod +x Proxalume Proxalume_Data/Application/Proxalume.App first) at the top level of the package. Nothing needs to be installed.

Unlocking a trial or license

In a commercially licensed build, open Help > License and Activation…. Proxalume automatically initializes an encrypted local device vault bound to your hardware: choose Start 14-day free trial with your email or enter your purchased PROX-... key and choose Activate / refresh online. See License and activation.

Your first analysis

  1. Choose File > Open Project (or File > Open Git Repository…) and pick a folder.
  2. Wait for the scan to finish; the status bar shows progress.
  3. Explore with the view tabs: 2D Graph, 3D Code City, Route Flow, Schema and Models, Findings and Security, Project Health, Impact and Diff, and Supply Chain.
  4. To study a compiled program instead, choose Binary > Open Binary… and start on the Triage tab; to start an incident investigation, choose Binary > New Forensic Case….

The topic Getting started: your first analysis walks through this step by step, and Keyboard shortcuts lists the shortcuts. Press F1 in the application for the same guide.

License and activation

All paid plans and the 14-day free trial include every desktop source-code, binary and forensic analysis feature. Your plan determines seats, personal device allowance, update maintenance window and support terms.

Local device vault initialization

In a commercially licensed build, Proxalume opens the Proxalume Studio Activation window at startup until an active trial or license is unlocked; you can also open it at any time from Help > License and Activation….

Proxalume automatically derives and manages an encrypted local device vault (device.vault) bound to persistent hardware characteristics of your workstation. You do not need to create or manage a separate device password. The device keypair remains securely stored on your local computer and is never transmitted across the network.

Option 1: Activating a purchased license key

After purchasing a plan on the website:

  1. Sign in to your website Customer Portal, open Licenses, and copy your PROX-... license key.
  2. Open Help > License and Activation….
  3. In Option 1: Activate Purchased License, paste your key into purchased license key (entering your account email is optional for reference).
  4. Enter a recognizable Device Nickname (for example Workstation or Studio-Laptop).
  5. Choose Activate / refresh online. Proxalume performs a cryptographic challenge-response check over HTTPS, binds the device slot in your customer portal, and stores a signed offline activation certificate inside your encrypted local vault.
  6. Choose Continue offline to begin using the workbench.

Option 2: Starting the 14-day free trial

To evaluate Proxalume before purchasing:

  1. Open Help > License and Activation….
  2. Under Option 2: Start 14-Day Free Trial, enter your email address into Account email for trial.
  3. Choose Start 14-day free trial. If your computer is online, Proxalume requests a signed 14-day trial certificate for this device from the licensing service (one free trial per device). If no network connection is available, a local offline evaluation begins immediately.
  4. Choose Continue offline to enter the workbench.

Once started, the 14-day trial runs completely offline with every desktop analysis feature enabled and ends automatically after 14 days. The trial tracks monotonic time locally: setting the system clock backward by more than a few minutes permanently ends the trial on that device. When you are ready to purchase, choose Buy license to open the pricing page in your browser, then activate your license key in the same window without reinstalling.

Offline operation and air-gapped workstations

After activation, unlocking your vault and verifying your license happen entirely on your computer with zero background network heartbeats:

  • Perpetual licenses carry no expiration date for entitled releases and run offline indefinitely without ever needing to reconnect to the internet.
  • Time-limited or annual licenses work offline until their stated validity date expires.
  • Optional online actions—such as checking for updates, cloning remote Git repositories or querying online vulnerability advisories—only connect when you ask them to. Account changes or revocations made on the website take effect on a disconnected computer the next time it refreshes online.

Perpetual entitlement and update maintenance

Every perpetual purchase includes 12 months of updates and maintenance:

  • Any release published on or before your Maintenance through date remains permanently usable on your perpetual license, even years after your maintenance window ends.
  • Installing a release published after your maintenance date requires active maintenance (see Updates).
  • After renewing maintenance or upgrading your plan on the website, open Help > License and Activation… while online and choose Activate / refresh online to download your updated entitlement certificate. If a network request fails or is canceled with Cancel request, your existing saved activation is preserved untouched.

Seats, device allowance and moving to another computer

Standard Individual and Pro seats allow activation on up to 2 personal computers per licensed user (for example a desktop and a laptop) and allow up to 5 self-service device slot transfers per license in any 30-day period, so you can replace hardware without contacting support. Support can move a device beyond that limit (enforced in LicensingService::deactivate; staff are exempt). Organization plans let administrators invite team members and assign seats from the website Customer Portal.

To move an activation to a new computer:

  1. On the old computer while online, open Help > License and Activation…, tick Free this device slot and end this licensed session., and choose Deactivate this device. This releases the device slot immediately and closes the licensed session.
  2. Install Proxalume on the new computer, open the activation dialog, and activate your license key there.

If you replace your workstation, reformat a drive, or lose access to the old computer, sign in to your website Customer Portal, open Licenses, deactivate the old device slot there, and then activate on your replacement installation. Never copy device.vault files between computers: each vault is bound to its own device keypair.

Clock checks, privacy and command-line limits

  • If Proxalume reports an invalid system clock date, correct your operating system's date and time zone and try again.
  • Activation requests send only your license key, the public key of your local device vault, the device name you entered and the application version over HTTPS. No source code, binary files, file paths or project names are ever transmitted. Never include license keys or device.vault files in a bug report.
  • Unattended licensed command-line sessions in headless environments are not supported: activation credentials are never accepted on the command line or in environment variables so they cannot leak into shell history or process listings.

Welcome to Proxalume

Proxalume is a desktop application that helps you understand software you did not write, or wrote long ago. It reads a project's files without running them, draws the relationships it finds as a map, lists possible problems, and (in the Binary Workbench) lets you look inside compiled programs.

Everything runs on your own computer. The application does not need an internet connection, and it does not send your code anywhere. (The optional AI assistant talks only to an endpoint you configure; it is off by default. See Settings.)

What problems it helps with

  • "What does this codebase contain, and how do the pieces connect?" Open a project folder and explore a graph of files, classes, functions, routes and database tables.
  • "Is anything here risky?" The Findings view lists security and quality signals with the file, line and evidence behind each one.
  • "What did this change affect?" Save a snapshot of an analysis and compare it later, or compare against Git history.
  • "What does this depend on, and is any of it known to be vulnerable?" The Supply Chain view lists dependencies from lockfiles, exports an SBOM and looks up published advisories.
  • "What is inside this program file?" The Binary Workbench shows a compiled file's format, strings, functions and control flow without executing it.

Who it is for

  • Developers joining an unfamiliar project.
  • Reviewers checking a change or auditing a codebase.
  • Security and reverse-engineering beginners who want to inspect a program file safely.

You do not need to know how the application is built. Terms are explained when they first appear, and there is a Glossary.

Source analysis versus binary analysis

Source-code analysisBinary analysis
InputA folder of source files (PHP, JavaScript/TypeScript, C#, Python, Java, C/C++, SQL, JSON/YAML...)A single compiled file (Windows PE, Linux ELF, macOS Mach-O) or a raw firmware image
You getA graph of symbols and relationships, findings, health and coverage numbersHashes, entropy, strings, imports, functions, disassembly, control-flow graphs
WhereMain views: 2D Graph, 3D Code City, Findings and othersThe Binary Workbench view and the Binary menu
Runs the code?NoNo

The two areas are separate: opening a binary does not change your open project, and the other way around.

What it can and cannot tell you

Important Every result comes from automatic static analysis. It is evidence to investigate, not proof. A relationship may be missing because a language feature is not understood. A finding may be a false alarm. An empty findings list does not mean the software is secure.

The application tells you how much it analyzed: see How analysis works and Project Health.

A tour of the main window

From top to bottom:

  1. Menu bar - File, Edit, View, Analyze, Binary and Help. Every action is reachable here, including File > Open Git Repository, File > Open Recent, the graph tools under View, and snapshots, Git comparison and the AI helpers under Analyze. See Keyboard shortcuts.
  2. Toolbar - Open Project (with a ▾ list of recent projects), Open Binary, Rescan (and Cancel while a scan runs), Settings, a filter box for the graph, export buttons (JSON, CSV, SARIF, DOT), the command palette ⌘, a Light/Dark theme switch ◐ and ? for this guide.
  3. View tabs - 2D Graph, 3D Code City, Route Flow, Schema and Models, Findings and Security, Project Health, Impact and Diff, Vulnerability Scanner, Hex Editor, Binary Workbench and Supply Chain.
  4. Left panel (Repository Explorer) - a file tree with a filter box for name, path or language.
  5. Centre - the active view.
  6. Right panel (Element Inspector) - details of whatever you selected: kind, language, file, line, complexity, relationships and a read-only source preview. It also holds the Settings & scan options and AI assistant sections.
  7. Status bar - the current status message, a progress bar and Cancel button while a scan runs, the project path, and counts of analyzed files, nodes, edges and findings.

The Help menu contains Documentation (this guide), Quick Start, Guide Topics, Keyboard Shortcuts, Full Reference (HTML), Open Data Folder, Copy Diagnostic Info and About. Help > About shows the version, build details, privacy statement and open-source credits.

Using this guide

  • Use the search box at the top left of the guide window to search all topics. Results open the matching section.
  • Use Back, Forward and Home to move between pages.
  • Return to application minimizes the guide so the main window comes to the front. Press F1 or choose Help > Documentation to bring the guide back.
  • Links that begin with a button label such as "Open Settings" run the matching action in the main window; your project and analysis stay as they are.
  • Each page ends with related links. Problems are collected in Troubleshooting.

Getting started: your first analysis

This tutorial takes about ten minutes. It uses the small sample project that ships with the application source (samples/LaravelShopFixture), a tiny Laravel shop with routes, controllers and models, so you do not need to prepare anything.

Note The sample folder is part of the source repository, not of the downloaded program package. If you only have the packaged application, use any small folder of source code instead; every step is the same.

1. Launch the application

  • Windows: extract the package and run Proxalume.exe.
  • Linux: extract the .tar.gz and run ./Proxalume (a desktop session is required).

The main window opens with an empty graph and a "No repository open" panel on the left. If it does not open, see Troubleshooting.

2. Open a project

  1. Choose File > Open Project (or press Ctrl+O, or click Open Project in the toolbar).
  2. In the folder picker, select the folder to analyze, for example the sample LaravelShopFixture folder, and confirm.

The application scans the folder. While it works, the status bar shows progress. To stop, click Cancel in the status bar; the status line then reads that the scan was cancelled, and you can start again with Rescan. When it finishes, the status bar shows counts such as Analyzed: N files, Nodes, Edges and Findings.

To analyze a public repository from GitHub instead, choose File > Open Git Repository… and paste its address; see Opening a Git repository.

Projects you open appear under Recent projects in the left panel next time, so you can reopen them with one click. Clear Recent Projects empties the list; it never touches your files.

3. Understand what you are looking at

  • The 2D Graph shows components as colored boxes (nodes) joined by lines (edges). The Legend in the left of the graph explains the colors.
  • Click a node. The Element Inspector on the right shows its kind, language, file, line, complexity and its incoming and outgoing relationships. See Exploring the 2D graph.
  • Open the Findings and Security tab to see possible problems, then select one to see its evidence. See Findings and security.
  • Open Project Health to see how much of the project was analyzed. See Project Health.

4. Try the other views

Use the tabs or the View menu: 3D Code City, Route Flow and Schema, Impact and Diff, and the Vulnerability Scanner list.

5. Change a setting and rescan

If a file was skipped or you want to exclude a folder, open Settings (Edit > Settings), adjust, then use File > Rescan (Ctrl+R) to analyze again. Results are cached by file content, so unchanged files are reused and the rescan is quick.

6. Export a result

Click JSON, CSV, SARIF or DOT in the toolbar, or use File > Export. Files are written to an exports folder inside the project you opened. See Search, exports and reports for what each contains and what to check before sharing.

7. Close safely

The application does not modify your project when you analyze it. Closing the window (or File > Exit) is safe at any time; settings, recent projects, finding suppressions and snapshots are saved as you go. If a scan is running, cancel it first. Hex edits and binary patches are the only features that can change files, and only when you explicitly press their Save or Apply buttons (see Annotating, patching and the hex editor).

Saving and restoring your work

  • Settings, recent projects and suppressions are restored automatically at the next start.
  • Snapshots (Impact and Diff tab) save an analysis you can compare with later.
  • Binary sessions (Binary Workbench > Session & Hex) save your binary investigation.
  • There is no single "save workspace" file for the whole window layout or the current graph selection in this version.

Tutorials

Help > Tutorials opens step-by-step walkthroughs with a picture for every step: a first look at the main window, and opening a project and reading its results. Choose one on the left, then use Next and Back (or the arrow keys). The tutorials work offline and the window stays open while you try each step in the application.

You can also start the application with a folder name (Proxalume.exe C:\work\myproject) to open and scan that folder straight away.

Next: Opening projects and repositories.

Opening projects and repositories

Local folders

File > Open Project (Ctrl+O) analyzes a folder that is already on your computer. The folder is only read. This is the only way to open source code in the current version.

You can also reopen a folder from File > Open Recent, from the ▾ button next to Open Project in the toolbar, or from Recent projects (left panel when nothing is open).

Opening a Git repository

File > Open Git Repository… (Ctrl+Shift+O) clones a repository from GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket or any other Git server into a folder you choose and opens it. You can pick a branch, tag or exact commit, and optionally a shallow clone. See Opening a Git repository for the full steps, private repositories, and keeping a clone up to date.

Things to know when you import a repository:

  • Git must be installed. The application uses it to do the download.
  • For private repositories, sign in outside this application (Git Credential Manager, GitHub CLI or an SSH key). Never put a token inside an address, a project file, a settings box, a screenshot or a bug report. The application has no field for tokens and refuses addresses that contain one.
  • Submodules and Git LFS large files are not downloaded automatically. Their code is not analyzed until you choose File > Git Repository > Download Submodules or Download Large Files (Git LFS); Repository Info… tells you when they are present.
  • Uncommitted changes in the folder are analyzed as they are on disk, and the application never discards them. The Working tree changes list in Settings & scan options shows what Git considers changed.
  • A folder you opened with File > Open Project that is already a Git clone gets the same File > Git Repository actions.

Several folders at once (additional roots)

Open the right-hand panel section Settings & scan options and use Add Root to merge another folder into the same graph, for example a backend and a frontend that live in separate folders. Remove Selected and Clear All undo that. Roots are merged into one searchable graph. You can also type roots separated by semicolons in the box above the list, or in Settings.

Choosing an analysis scope

The scope of an analysis is the opened folder plus any additional roots, minus exclusions. There are no separate "profiles". To narrow the scope:

  • Open a sub-folder instead of the whole repository.
  • Add custom exclusions in Settings (semicolon-separated names or patterns).
  • Lower max file size or max directory depth in Settings.

Built-in exclusions such as node_modules and vendor are listed in Project Health > Excluded Directories, so you can always see what was left out.

Git comparison

The Git comparison part of Settings & scan options compares the working tree or two revisions. It reads your local .git data only. See Change impact.

Checking which revision you opened

Use File > Git Repository > Repository Info…. It shows the remote address, the branch or detached commit, the commit id, whether history is shallow, local changes, and how far ahead or behind the remote you are. Projects opened through Open Git Repository also show the revision in the status bar.

Common problems

  • Folder picker shows nothing or the project will not open: Troubleshooting.
  • Clone errors: see Troubleshooting.

Next: How repository analysis works.

Opening a Git repository

File > Open Git Repository… (Ctrl+Shift+O) downloads a repository from GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket or any other Git server into a folder you choose and opens it like any other project. You do not need to use a terminal. The same button is on the start panel when no project is open.

What you need

  • Git installed on your computer (https://git-scm.com/downloads). The application uses it to do the download. If Git is missing, the window says so.
  • An internet connection only for the download. Everything after that is offline.
  • Public repositories need no account.

Step by step

  1. Choose File > Open Git Repository….
  2. Paste the repository address into Repository address, for example https://github.com/octocat/Hello-World. The line under the box tells you whether it is accepted.
  3. Optional: click Load branches and tags to list what the repository offers, then pick one under Branch or tag. Leave it on Default branch to get the repository's main branch. To analyze one exact version, type its id (7 to 40 hexadecimal characters) under Commit.
  4. Check the Destination. A folder inside Documents/Proxalume/Repositories is suggested (or inside the folder you chose under Settings > Files and editor); use Browse… to choose another place. The folder must not exist yet, or must be empty.
  5. Optional: tick or untick Shallow clone (its starting state is a setting) to download only the latest snapshot. It is faster and smaller, but the history is missing, so Git-aware features such as comparing commits have little to work with.
  6. Click Clone and Open. A progress bar shows the download; Cancel stops it.
  7. When it finishes, the project opens and the normal analysis runs. The status bar shows the remote address and the revision, for example main @ 7fd1a60, and (shallow) when history is limited.

If the destination already holds a clone of the same repository, the application simply opens it as it is. It never downloads over existing files.

Addresses that work

You typeResult
https://github.com/owner/repositoryThe default branch
https://github.com/owner/repository.gitThe same
github.com/owner/repositoryThe same (https is assumed)
https://github.com/owner/repository/tree/branch-nameThat branch is preselected
https://github.com/owner/repository/commit/<id>That commit is filled in
https://github.com/owner/repository/releases/tag/v1.2.3That tag is preselected
https://gitlab.com/group/subgroup/projectGitLab, including nested groups
https://gitlab.com/group/project/-/tree/branch-nameThat branch is preselected (/-/commit/<id> and /-/tags/<tag> work too)
https://bitbucket.org/team/repositoryBitbucket
https://git.example.com/team/repository.gitAny other server, including your own (a custom port such as :8443 is accepted for these)
git@github.com:owner/repository.gitSSH, using your own SSH key (see below)
ssh://git@git.example.com:2222/team/repository.gitSSH with a port

These are refused, with an explanation: addresses that contain a user name, password or token, http:// addresses, schemes other than https and ssh, host names that could be read as a command option, and names with unusual characters.

Private repositories

The application never asks for a password or token and has no place to store one. To open a private repository:

  1. Sign in outside this application, using one of: Git Credential Manager (installed with Git for Windows), GitHub CLI (gh auth login), or an SSH key registered with your Git server.
  2. Use the normal https address, or the SSH address, here. Git will use the credentials you already set up.

For SSH addresses the application never waits for a typed password or a "trust this host?" question. If the connection is refused, run ssh -T git@host once in a terminal (this trusts the server and checks your key), then try again.

Warning Never type a token or password into the address. Such addresses are refused, because tokens in addresses end up in logs, history and screenshots.
Note Private-repository access depends on your own Git sign-in and has not been verified with every setup. If GitHub says the repository "does not exist or needs sign-in", check the address and your sign-in with git ls-remote <address> in a terminal; the two cases look the same to Git.

Keeping a clone up to date

With a Git project open, File > Git Repository offers:

  • Fetch Updates - downloads new commits without changing your files. The status bar says how many are waiting.
  • Update (Fast-Forward) - moves the branch forward to the fetched commits, then rescans. It stops without changing anything if the branch has diverged.
  • Switch Branch, Tag or Commit… - changes the checked-out revision, then rescans.
  • Download Submodules - fetches the submodules the repository lists, then rescans. Only plain https addresses are followed (a submodule that asks for SSH, git://, a local path or plain http is refused with an explanation and nothing is downloaded).
  • Download Large Files (Git LFS) - downloads the contents of large files that are only pointers, then rescans. It needs Git LFS to be installed (https://git-lfs.com), and refuses a repository whose .lfsconfig names a file server that is not https. Large downloads can take a while; the status bar shows progress.
  • Repository Info… - shows the remote, revision, whether history is shallow, local changes, how far ahead or behind the remote you are, and submodule and large-file status.

Update and Switch are refused when you have uncommitted changes. The application never discards, resets or overwrites your work; commit or stash with Git first.

Submodules and large files

The download does not fetch submodules (other repositories nested inside) and does not download Git LFS large files. Repository Info tells you when they exist. Their code is not analyzed until you choose File > Git Repository > Download Submodules or Download Large Files (Git LFS) (you can also run git submodule update --init and git lfs pull yourself) and rescan. Large files that were not downloaded appear as small pointer text files. Nothing is downloaded unless you ask.

Safety

  • The repository is treated as untrusted. Nothing in it is run: no build scripts, package scripts or Git hooks.
  • Error messages and logs have any credentials removed.
  • A clone that fails or is cancelled removes only what it created. A folder that existed before is never deleted.

What is not supported

SSH addresses; hosts other than github.com; downloading submodules or LFS files without being asked; submodules that use SSH or other non-https addresses; sparse or partial clones; showing GitHub issues or pull requests; and saving credentials.

If something goes wrong

See Troubleshooting. Related: Opening projects, Change impact.

Source-code analysis

How repository analysis works

When you open a project, the application reads the supported files in the folder, works out how the pieces relate (including links across languages, for example a JavaScript fetch('/api/orders') call and the Laravel route that serves it), and then produces findings, health numbers and coverage numbers.

Your code is read, never executed.

Which languages are understood

Language / file typeWhat is extracted
PHP and LaravelClasses, interfaces, traits, methods, Composer namespaces, routes, controller actions, middleware, Eloquent relationships, migrations, Blade templates
JavaScript / TypeScriptES modules, require(), classes, exported functions, fetch/axios calls to backend routes
C#Classes, records, interfaces, using directives, method calls, complexity
PythonModules, imports, classes, functions, calls, complexity
JavaPackages, imports, classes, interfaces, enums, methods, inheritance
C and C++#include headers, structs, classes, functions
SQLCREATE TABLE, columns, foreign keys
JSON, YAML, .env.exampleConfiguration keys and missing-variable checks

The exact capability list, including which analyzers are "partial", can be saved with File > Export > Analyzer Capabilities JSON.

Limitation Some files can only be analyzed in a simpler way. Those results are marked as partly analyzed, and the application keeps working.

Three kinds of relationship evidence

Every edge in the graph records how it was found. The kind is shown when you select the edge.

EvidenceIn plain wordsHow much to trust it
DeclaredWritten directly in the code, such as an import, extends or use line. This is a syntactic relationship.High: it is exactly what the file says
ResolvedThe exact target could be determined, for example which method an overloaded call refers to.High where the analyzer supports it
InferredDerived from conventions or patterns, for example "this model probably maps to that table because of its name".Medium: a good lead, not a fact
PotentialA heuristic guess, such as a string that looks like a route name. Drawn as a dashed line.Low: always confirm in the source
UnresolvedThe code points at something the analyzer could not find.Informational: the target may be outside the project

A heuristic is a rule of thumb that is usually right but can be wrong.

Why some files are not fully analyzed

Each file ends in one of these states (counts are on Project Health):

  • Analyzed - fully parsed and extracted.
  • Partially analyzed - symbols were extracted, but with limits (for example a language feature the analyzer does not follow, or a very large file).
  • Skipped - deliberately not analyzed: inside an excluded directory, larger than the maximum file size, or deeper than the maximum directory depth.
  • Unsupported - no analyzer exists for this file type.
  • Failed - the file could not be read or parsed; the failure is isolated so the rest of the scan continues.

Parse errors appear in Findings and Security as findings so you can see which file and line.

How exclusions and settings change results

  • Built-in exclusions skip folders such as .git, bin, obj, node_modules, vendor, dist, build, coverage and a few others. They are listed in Project Health.
  • .gitignore files are not read; use custom exclusions in Settings instead.
  • Max file size, max directory depth, semantic analysis and scan concurrency are in Settings. Turning semantic analysis off makes scanning faster but reduces resolved relationships.
  • After you change a setting that affects scanning, run Rescan. Results for files that have not changed are reused to save time.

Reading coverage

On Project Health, compare Discovered files with Analyzed files. If analyzed is much lower, look at the partially analyzed, skipped, unsupported and failed tiles. Coverage tells you how much of the project the findings and the graph are based on. A graph built from 40% of the files shows 40% of the picture.

Important An analysis result reflects what the relevant analyzers can understand. Dynamic code (code that builds names at run time, reflection, plug-ins loaded from disk) is often invisible to static analysis.

Next: Exploring the 2D graph.

Exploring the 2D graph

The 2D Graph (View > 2D Graph) is the main map of your project. Each box is a node (a file, class, function, route, table...). Each line is an edge (a relationship such as "calls", "imports", "inherits from" or "routes to"). Together they form the code graph.

Use it when you want to answer "what depends on this?", "what does this touch?" or "how does a request get from here to there?".

Move around

To do thisDo this
Zoom in or outUse the mouse wheel, or the Zoom In / Zoom Out buttons at the top right of the graph
Fit everything on screenFit to View
Pan (move the picture)Drag on empty space with the left mouse button, or hold Ctrl and drag, or drag with the middle button
Select a nodeClick it. Its details open in the Element Inspector on the right
Select a relationshipClick an edge, or click a relationship button in the inspector's Relationships list

The Legend at the bottom left explains the node colors.

Find things

  • Filter the graph: type in the toolbar box ("Filter graph by symbol, route or file"). The graph, Route Flow list and Schema list narrow to matches. Click the ✕ next to the box or Reset Filters to clear it.
  • Search all symbols: press Ctrl+F to focus the quick search in the left panel, then pick a result to select it. See Search, exports and reports.
  • Browse files: the Repository Explorer tree on the left lists files; the filter box above it filters by file name, path or language. Selecting a file selects its node.

Focus on part of the graph

  1. Select a node.
  2. Click Isolate Neighbourhood to show only that node and the nodes directly connected to it.
  3. Click Reset Filters to bring everything back.

Isolating one node shows only its direct neighbours, not their neighbours. Select a neighbour and isolate again to walk outward step by step.

Find a path between two components

  1. Select the starting node and click ① Set Path Start.
  2. Select the target node and click → Find Path to Selected.
  3. The path is highlighted and a summary (number of steps, nodes on the way) appears under the buttons.
  4. ✕ Clear Path removes the highlight.

The path follows relationship direction (from the start to the target). "No path" means the application found no chain of known relationships; it does not prove the two parts never interact at run time.

Spot dependency cycles

A dependency cycle means A depends on B, and B (directly or through others) depends back on A. Nodes that are part of a cycle are marked in the graph, and the full list is on Project Health. See Project Health, cycles and architecture rules.

Inspect the evidence behind a relationship

Click an edge, or choose one in the inspector. The Selected relationship box shows the relationship, how it was found (its evidence) and, where known, the source location. Dashed lines are heuristic ("potential") relationships.

Go to the source code

With a node or relationship selected:

  • The inspector shows a read-only source code preview.
  • Open in Editor opens the file at the right line in your editor. Configure the editor command in Settings. If no command is set, the file opens with the system's default program for that file type (the line number is only used when your editor command contains {line}). If the command fails, a message tells you to check it.
  • On a relationship, Open source location jumps to where the relationship is written.

Tips

  • Large projects can contain thousands of nodes. Filter or isolate first, then zoom.
  • If something you expect is missing, check Project Health to see whether the file was analyzed.
  • AI Explain is available only if you enabled the optional local AI assistant in Settings.

Next: 3D Code City, Route Flow and Schema.

The 3D Code City, Route Flow and Schema views

These views show the same analysis as the graph in different ways. All of them are read-only.

3D Code City

View > 3D Code City draws your project as a small city. Each building is a component: the taller the building, the larger or more complex the code. Components of the same kind and language are grouped into districts.

Use it for a fast overview of where the big, complex parts of a project are.

  1. Open the 3D Code City tab.
  2. Click a building to select it. Its details appear in the Element Inspector, exactly as in the 2D graph.
  3. Use the buttons at the top right:
  4. Rotate Left / Rotate Right turn the camera.
  5. Reset Camera returns to the default view.
  6. Toggle Height Mode switches what height means (for example lines of code or complexity).
  7. Toggle Color Mode switches between coloring by kind and by language.
  8. Toggle Wireframe shows outlines, which helps when buildings hide each other.
  9. The slider ("LOD Nodes") limits how many buildings are drawn. Lower it if the view is slow.
Note A tall building means "large or complex", not "bad". Complexity here is a count of decision points in the code (cyclomatic complexity) and says nothing about correctness.

Route Flow

View > Route Flow lists the web request pipeline discovered in Laravel projects: routes, middleware, controllers, services, models and views. Each row shows the kind, the label, the controller (where known) and the file.

It is built from static route definitions, not from a running application, so it cannot show routes created dynamically at run time. Select a row to inspect it. The toolbar filter box narrows the list.

If your project is not a Laravel project, this list may be empty. That is expected.

Schema and Models

View > Schema and Models lists database tables, columns, migrations and the models mapped to them, taken from migrations, SQL files and naming conventions. The association is static evidence; the application does not connect to a database.

When the views look empty

Open Project Health to check whether the relevant files were analyzed, and see Troubleshooting.

Findings and security

What a finding is

A finding (also called a diagnostic) is something the analyzers noticed that deserves a human look: a possible security weakness, a code-quality signal, a parse error, or a structural observation such as a database table without a primary key.

Important A finding is a potential issue, not a confirmed vulnerability. It says "this pattern is often dangerous". Whether it is exploitable depends on how the code is used. Conversely, no findings does not mean the software is secure, especially when coverage is incomplete.

Open the list

Choose View > Findings and Security (or the tab). Each row shows:

  • the rule id (for example SEC001),
  • the severity: Info, Warning or Error,
  • the message and a short piece of evidence (the code or fact that triggered it),
  • the file, the line, and a SUPPRESSED label when you have hidden it.

Select a row to see the full finding in the Element Inspector, including the source preview.

Severity and confidence

Severity (Info, Warning, Error) says how serious the problem would be if real, and it is what the list shows and filters on. Analyzers also keep an internal confidence score for how sure they are that the pattern is really there (for example higher when a variable that came from user input reaches a dangerous call). The list does not display that score, so read the evidence text: a finding whose evidence shows user input flowing into the risky call deserves more attention than a bare keyword match. The input check is deliberately simple and can miss paths or flag safe ones.

Rules included

The built-in security rules cover, among others:

RuleLooks for
SEC001Possible SQL injection from string concatenation in raw SQL
SEC002Dynamic code execution such as eval, system, exec, shell_exec
SEC003Unsafe deserialization such as unserialize
SEC004Hard-coded credentials and API keys
SEC005File paths built from request input
SEC006HTML forms in Blade views without @csrf

Python, Java, C# and C/C++ analyzers add language-specific rules (for example eval/pickle in Python, Runtime.exec in Java, strcpy/gets in C). There is no screen for adding your own rules in this version.

Filter findings

  • Severity box: choose All severities, Info, Warning or Error.
  • Show suppressed: tick to include findings you have suppressed.
  • The Visible counter shows how many findings match.

Suppress and restore a finding

Suppress findings you have reviewed and decided are not relevant (for example a test fixture).

  1. Select the finding.
  2. Click Suppress selected (or Edit > Suppress Selected Finding).
  3. It disappears from the default list. Tick Show suppressed to see it again, labeled SUPPRESSED.
  4. To bring it back, select it and click Restore selected (or Edit > Restore Selected Finding).

Suppressions are remembered between sessions in your user profile. They do not change your source files.

Warning Suppression hides a finding from your view and exports. It does not fix anything. Record why you suppressed it elsewhere if others rely on your report.

Compare with a baseline

To see only what changed, save a baseline snapshot and compare later: new, resolved and persistent findings are reported. See Change impact.

The Vulnerability Scanner tab

Vulnerability Scanner is a simple list of all findings across all analyzers (rule id, message, file) in red cards. It is read-only and does not have the filters of the Findings tab. There is no online vulnerability database lookup: it reports what the local rules found.

Export findings

Use SARIF (toolbar or File > Export > SARIF) to give findings to other tools, CSV for a spreadsheet and Markdown for a readable report. See Search, exports and reports, including what to check before sharing.

Next: Project Health, cycles and architecture rules.

Project Health, cycles and architecture rules

View > Project Health answers "how much of my project did the application actually understand, and what does its structure look like?"

Coverage tiles

TileMeaning
Analyzed FilesFiles fully parsed and extracted
Discovered FilesAll files found in the active tree (after exclusions)
Graph NodesClasses, routes, functions and other symbols in the graph
RelationshipsCalls, routes, references and other edges
Security and ErrorsActionable findings
Partially AnalyzedSymbols were extracted with limits
Skipped / UnsupportedNot analyzed because of an exclusion, size or depth limit, or because no analyzer exists
Failed FilesFiles that could not be read or parsed; the failure is isolated

Below the tiles are breakdowns of Nodes by Kind, Relationships by Evidence (see evidence kinds) and Languages.

How to interpret coverage: divide Analyzed by Discovered. A high number gives the graph and findings more weight; a low number means you are looking at a partial picture. Skipped and failed tiles tell you where to look next (settings, file size, unsupported formats).

Excluded directories

The Excluded Directories list shows which folders were left out (for example node_modules, vendor, bin, obj, .git). Add your own in Settings under Custom exclusions, then rescan.

Dependency cycles

The Detected Dependency Cycles and Recursive Paths list shows groups of components that depend on each other in a loop: modules importing each other, call chains that return to their start, and so on. The nodes involved are also marked in the 2D graph.

Note A cycle is a structural observation, not automatically a bug. Direct recursion is often intentional. Cycles between layers or modules are worth reviewing because they make code harder to change and test.

To review one: note a node from the list, find it in the 2D graph, select it and inspect its relationships.

Architecture rules (optional policy file)

The application can check that components only depend on what you allow, for example "controllers may use services and models, but not repositories directly". If a relationship breaks a rule, a finding is reported so you can see architecture drift (the design slowly diverging from what was intended).

By default a built-in policy is used (for example Controller to Service/Model/View, Service to Repository/Model, Repository to Model/Table). To supply your own:

  1. Create a file named architecture-policy.json in the project root (or in a .opencode folder inside it), or choose any path in Settings & scan options > architecture-policy.json path.
  2. Use this shape, where each key is a kind of component and its list holds the kinds it may depend on:
{
  "allowedDependencies": {
    "Controller": ["Service", "Model", "View"],
    "Service": ["Repository", "Model", "Service"],
    "Repository": ["Model", "DatabaseTable"]
  }
}
  1. Rescan. Violations appear in Findings and Security.

If the file is missing, unreadable or has no allowedDependencies, the built-in policy is used without an error message, so check that your rules appear to take effect. Rules apply only to component kinds that you list.

Next: Change impact.

Change impact: snapshots and Git comparison

Use these tools to answer "what changed, and what might that affect?"

Snapshots (Impact and Diff tab)

A snapshot is a saved copy of an analysis result, used as a baseline.

  1. Open and analyze your project.
  2. In Impact and Diff, click Save Baseline Snapshot.
  3. Later (after code has changed and you have rescanned), choose the snapshot in the Select Baseline Snapshot box and click Compare with Baseline.
  4. Read the results:
  5. Added Nodes and Removed Nodes - components that appeared or disappeared.
  6. Modified Components - components whose size (lines of code) or complexity changed, with the amounts.
  7. Directly Impacted and the list of callers and downstream targets - components that depend on, or are used by, what changed. This is the blast radius: the parts most likely to be affected.
  8. New, resolved and persistent findings compared with the baseline.
  9. Clear Comparison removes the comparison from view.

Snapshots are stored in your user profile (Snapshots folder under the application's data directory), not in your project.

Limitation Impact is computed from the relationships the analyzers found. Dependencies they cannot see (reflection, configuration-driven wiring, other services) are not included, so a short impact list is not proof of a safe change.

Git comparison

The right-hand panel's Settings & scan options > Git comparison compares revisions using your local Git history. It needs the git program installed and on your PATH, and the opened folder must be inside a Git repository.

  • Compare Working Tree to HEAD (Analyze menu): lists files you have changed and not yet committed.
  • Compare Git Range: type a base (for example main) and a target (HEAD, a commit id, or a range), then click Compare Git Range. The commit/range changes appear in the lists below the boxes.
  • Export Git Impact Report (Analyze menu or File > Export): writes git-impact-report.json to the project's exports folder.

Nothing in your repository is changed: the application only reads Git data.

If Git is not installed, the lists stay empty; see Troubleshooting.

Next: the Binary Workbench.

Supply chain: dependencies, SBOM, advisories and release checks

The Supply Chain view (View > Supply Chain) answers: what does this project depend on, which versions, what are their declared licenses, do known vulnerability reports mention them, and does a release folder still match what its build recorded?

Important This is an inventory read from files plus a lookup of published advisories. It does not prove the software is secure or complete. A package with no advisory may simply not have one yet, and a package with one may never run the vulnerable code.

Scan dependencies

  1. Open a project, open View > Supply Chain, and click Scan Dependencies.
  2. The application reads these files, wherever they are in the project:
EcosystemFiles readWhat you get
npmpackage-lock.json (version 2 or 3), else package.jsonExact versions, direct or transitive, development or production, hashes, declared license
Composer (PHP)composer.lock with composer.json, else composer.jsonExact versions, direct or transitive, development or production, declared license
NuGet (.NET)packages.lock.json, else obj/project.assets.json, else the project fileExact versions and dependency links from a lock or restore output; only declared versions from a project file alone
  1. Each row shows the package, version, Relation (direct means the project asked for it, transitive means it came along with something else), Scope, License (as declared), Resolution and Advisories.

Resolved means a lockfile or restore output records the exact version in use. Declared only means only a version constraint exists (for example ^1.2.0), so the installed version is unknown. The application never guesses a version from a constraint and never runs a package manager, a build or a script. To get a full inventory for a project that has only manifests, install its dependencies yourself (for example npm install) so a lockfile exists, then scan again.

Hover a row to see its package URL (purl), the standard identifier used in SBOMs.

What it cannot see

Installed-package folders (node_modules, vendor) are not read, so copied-in, vendored or dynamically loaded code is not listed. Other ecosystems (Java, Python, Go, Rust and others) are not read. Licenses are only those the lockfile or package metadata declares; many NuGet restores record none. Notes and limits of this inventory at the bottom of the view lists everything that was skipped or looked wrong.

Export an SBOM

An SBOM (software bill of materials) is a standard list of a program's components. Click Export CycloneDX SBOM to write exports/sbom.cdx.json in CycloneDX 1.6 JSON. The file keeps three things apart so nobody mistakes them:

  • resolved components (exact version known) and declared-only components (no version),
  • direct and transitive relationships (recorded as dependencies),
  • what the file does not know: it states that it is incomplete, and lists its sources and limitations.

An SBOM lists components. It does not say they are safe, and it does not say who built the software.

Compare with another SBOM

Compare with SBOM… imports a CycloneDX JSON file (versions 1.4 to 1.7) from a supplier, a build system or an earlier release, and compares it with the scan: identical, version differs, only in the SBOM, only in this project's files. Neither side is assumed complete, so a difference is a question to investigate, not a verdict.

Check advisories (known vulnerabilities)

Advisories come from the OSV database (https://osv.dev), which aggregates GitHub, npm, Packagist, NuGet and other advisory sources.

  • Check Advisories (online)… asks first, then sends only the ecosystem, package name and version of each resolved package to OSV over HTTPS. No source code, file names, project name or repository content is sent. Advisory records are cached on this computer with the time they were fetched.
  • Check Advisories (offline) uses only the cache and imported data.
  • Import Advisory Data… loads OSV-format JSON files (a single advisory, a list, or a {"vulns": [...]} file) for use without a network.

Each match shows the advisory id (and its CVE alias), severity as published, a summary, status and where the data came from.

Warning If the service cannot be reached, the view says so and shows only cached or imported data. A failed lookup is not a clean result.

Affected means the package version is covered by an advisory. It does not mean your code calls the vulnerable function; the application does not determine reachability.

From the command line

Proxalume --sbom path/to/project --out sbom.cdx.json
Proxalume --advisories path/to/project --out advisories.json
Proxalume --advisories path/to/project --offline --import advisories-folder

Exit codes: 0 success; 1 a finding to act on (an affected package); 2 the check could not be completed (bad input, or the advisory service was unavailable and nothing was cached), so no conclusion can be drawn.

Not available in this version

Not available Build provenance attestations (SLSA, in-toto) and their verification; digital-signature verification; matching packages to the contents of a compiled binary; license conflict analysis; importing test-coverage or runtime data; fuzzing; API contract comparison. These do not exist here, so nothing in the application pretends otherwise.

Related: Findings, Binary Workbench, Search and exports, Known gaps.

Start here

Rules, evidence, provenance, coverage and API contracts

The Analyze menu gathers the verification and evidence tools that tie source-code findings, custom security rules, test coverage, offline build attestations, runtime traces, fuzzing artifacts and API specifications into one auditable trail.

Unified rules and accepted findings

Choose Analyze > Rules and Accepted Findings… (or open the first tab of Analyze > Evidence, Provenance and Contracts…) to review findings across all three rule domains in one place:

  • ArchitecturePolicy ([ARCH]) — boundary violations from architecture-policy.json (see Project Health, cycles and architecture rules).
  • SecurityRulePack ([SEC]) — matches from built-in and custom regular-expression security rules.
  • AnalyzerDiagnostic ([DIAG]) — language analyzer warnings, risky API patterns and structural diagnostics.

Select any finding to inspect its domain, confidence, location, fingerprint and remediation guidance. Type a justification and choose Accept / Suppress to record acceptance locally (and export it to SARIF), or save and compare baselines across runs.

Writing custom security rules

Choose Analyze > Security Rule Editor… to author or edit a custom rule pack that runs on subsequent scans with bounded regular-expression timeouts, sample testing and instant active-pack registration.

Software evidence ledger

Open Analyze > Evidence, Provenance and Contracts… and select the Evidence Ledger tab. Every item carries an explicit certainty ceiling ([Exact], [StronglySupported], or [Guess]) and tracks file hashes on disk to flag modified artifacts [STALE].

Offline provenance and binary-to-package correlation

In the Provenance & Binary Link tab, inspect SLSA v0.2/v1.0 and in-toto DSSE attestations against local PEM public keys without transparency-log network calls, and correlate the open binary against lockfiles using the 4-rung Exact / Corroborated / Guess / None ladder.

Runtime traces, crash logs and fuzzing runs

In the Runtime & Fuzzing tab, import Chrome Trace, Speedscope, V8 .cpuprofile, folded stacks, crash logs and AFL++/libFuzzer/Go fuzzing directories as inert read-only evidence, or run bounded local fuzz harnesses with explicit confirmation.

Importing test coverage reports

Choose Analyze > Test Coverage… to overlay LCOV (.info), Cobertura XML, JaCoCo XML, Istanbul JSON or coverage.py JSON reports directly onto project files.

OpenAPI and Swagger API contract comparison

In the API Contract Diff tab, compare OpenAPI 3.0/3.1 or Swagger 2.0 specifications against previous revisions (separating breaking from additive changes) or compare specifications against discovered project HTTP routes.

Next: Workspace: panels, history and the command palette.

Workspace: panels, history and the command palette

This page covers how to arrange the main window and move around quickly. Everything described here is available today; the last section lists what is not.

Resize and hide the side panels

The main window has an Explorer panel on the left (project tree, search and filters) and an Inspector panel on the right (details of the selected item).

  • Resize: drag the thin divider between a panel and the central view. Widths are kept between 160 and 700 pixels.
  • Hide or show: View > Panels > Toggle Explorer Panel or Toggle Inspector Panel.
  • Reset: View > Panels > Reset Panel Layout returns both panels to their default widths (250 and 300) and shows them.
  • Keyboard: click a divider to focus it, then press Left or Right to move it in small steps.
  • Remembered: sizes and visibility are saved in your settings file and restored the next time the application starts. A damaged or older settings file falls back to the defaults.

Some views (Hex Editor, Binary Workbench and Supply Chain) use the whole window and show no side panels. Your panel choices come back when you return to another view.

Window layouts

View > Layouts remembers how you arranged the windows.

  • Save Current Layout... asks for a name and stores the main window's position and size, the side panels (shown or hidden, and their widths), the view and Binary Workbench tab in front, and every floating panel and tab with its position and size. Saving under an existing name asks before replacing it. You can keep up to 30 layouts.
  • Choose a saved layout from the list to apply it. Floating windows that are open are docked first, then the saved ones are opened where they were.
  • Delete a Layout removes one. Dock All Floating Windows brings every floating panel and tab back into the main window. Reset Window Layout docks everything, resets the panels and puts the main window back at its standard size in the middle of the screen.
  • The same actions are in the command palette (Ctrl+K).

Without saving anything, the application also remembers by itself: the main window reopens where it was, and a floating Explorer or Inspector is still floating. Turn this off with Settings > Startup > Remember my window layout. If a saved window position is on a monitor that is no longer connected, the window is moved back onto a screen you have.

Not included: dragging a floating window onto the main window to snap it into place. Floating tabs are brought back by applying a saved layout (they are not reopened automatically at start, because they need a binary open).

Back and forward in the Binary Workbench

While you investigate a binary, the application remembers the functions and addresses you visit.

ActionHow
Back to the previous locationBack button in the Binary Workbench header, Binary > Back to Previous Location, or Alt+Left
Forward to the next locationBinary > Forward to Next Location, or Alt+Right

Selecting an address inside the function you are already viewing refines the current location instead of adding a new entry. Going back and then visiting somewhere new discards the forward entries, as in a web browser. The history holds the latest 200 locations and is cleared when you open a different binary.

Save and reopen a workspace

File > Save Workspace As... saves a small workspace file that remembers your project, the binary you were studying, the view and tab you were on, the selected function and the panel layout. File > Open Workspace... restores them.

  • The file holds no file contents and no annotations; annotations are already saved per binary.
  • If the binary has changed since the workspace was saved (its contents are different), it is not reopened and the status bar says so.
  • A project folder or binary that no longer exists is reported and skipped; nothing is guessed.
  • A raw firmware image opened with custom settings is reopened with automatic detection, because the raw settings are not stored.

Command palette

Press Ctrl+K (or Edit > Command Palette or the toolbar button) and type part of what you want to do, for example graph, theme or binary.

  • Each result shows its category, its shortcut (only shortcuts that really exist) and how it matched: exact, starts with, word match, contains, keyword/category, or fuzzy (the letters you typed appear in order).
  • Up and Down choose a result, Enter runs it, Esc closes the palette.
  • Commands that cannot run right now (for example Back with no history) are shown dimmed and are not run.
  • Every command in the palette is a real menu action; the list is built from one registry so a shortcut is never listed twice.

Not available

These are not part of the application and are not described as steps: docking of panels next to each other, split panes showing two views at once, several documents open in tabs, user-defined keyboard shortcuts, snapping a floating window into place by dragging it, workspace files that also carry annotations or raw-image settings, and synchronized scrolling between views.

Advanced tools: workflows, extensions, archives, similar functions, floating panels, project settings and the debugger

Each tool below is available from the menus or the Command Palette (Ctrl+K). The last section lists what they do not do.

Floating panels

View > Panels > Float / Dock Explorer (or Inspector) moves that panel into its own window, for example onto a second monitor. Close the window, or choose the same item again, to dock it back. The panel keeps its selection and scroll position. A floating window reopens where you last left it, and with Settings > Startup > Remember my window layout on, the Explorer or Inspector is still floating the next time the application starts. See Window layouts.

Floating Binary Workbench tabs

In the Binary Workbench, Float this tab (or Binary > Float or Dock the Current Binary Workbench Tab in the Command Palette) shows the current sub-tab in its own window. Any number of tabs can float at once, so you can put the function list beside the strings, or the Types tab beside the hex view, by arranging the windows yourself. The tab shows a note while it is away; choose Float this tab again, or close the window, to bring it back. Each tab reopens where you last left it; to bring a whole arrangement of floating tabs back at once, save it as a layout (see Window layouts).

Project settings

A project can carry its own scan settings in .proxalume/settings.json. Because a project (for example a cloned repository) is not trusted, it can only make an analysis stricter and never looser:

  • exclusions: extra folders or names to skip (added to yours, at most 200).
  • maxFileSizeBytes, maxDirectoryDepth: used only if lower than your own limits.
  • enableSemanticAnalysis: false turns it off; true is ignored.
  • architecturePolicyPath: a file inside the project, used only if you have not chosen a policy yourself.

Everything the project changed is listed in the status bar (Project settings applied, hover for details) so a project can never change an analysis silently. Broken, oversized or linked settings files are ignored with a reason. Your own settings stay in your user settings file.

Workflows

Analyze > Run Workflow... lists saved sequences of steps and runs one, showing each step's result. Built in: Full source review, Export project data and Binary quick report. Your own workflows are JSON files in %APPDATA%/Proxalume/workflows:

{ "name": "My review", "stopOnError": true, "steps": ["rescan", "supply-scan", "show-view:4"] }

Steps come from a fixed list: rescan, supply-scan, export-json, binary-report, show-view:0 to show-view:10. A workflow can never run a program or script, so a workflow file from someone else is safe to open. Cancel stops after the current step.

Extensions

Binary > Extensions... shows installed extensions and applies their string rules to the open binary. An extension is a folder in %APPDATA%/Proxalume/extensions with an extension.json:

{ "id": "my-rules", "name": "My rules", "version": "1.0",
  "stringRules": [ { "name": "URL", "pattern": "https?://[a-z0-9./-]+" } ],
  "workflows": [ { "name": "Mine", "steps": ["rescan"] } ] }

Extensions contain data only: they cannot run code, read files or use the network. Patterns are simple text patterns; very complex ones are not accepted. Every match names the extension and rule that produced it, and a match is a hint, not a verdict. To remove an extension, delete its folder.

Plug-ins

Binary > Plug-ins (sandboxed programs)... lists the plug-ins you have installed and runs one on the open binary. A plug-in is a folder in %APPDATA%/Proxalume/plugins, such as plugins/my-scanner, holding:

  • plugin.wasm, the program, in WebAssembly form.
  • plugin.json (optional), with a name, description and version that the list shows.

Choose a plug-in, then Run on the open binary. The findings appear with their severity (info, low, medium or high), an address and a message, followed by anything the plug-in wrote to its log. Add findings to my notes copies the findings that have an address into your notes as comments (up to 200 per run, never replacing a comment you wrote; it adds to it). A finding is a lead for you to check, not a verdict. To remove a plug-in, delete its folder.

What a plug-in can and cannot do

A plug-in runs inside a sandbox that this application implements itself. It can compute, read the bytes of the open binary, read the list of functions (with your renames), and report findings and log lines. It cannot read or write your files, use the network, start programs, read the clock or see anything else on the computer, and it cannot change the open binary. Its limits are fixed: about 300 million instructions, 16 MB of memory, 400 nested calls, 20 seconds, 2,000 findings and 500 log lines. A plug-in that goes over a limit, does something invalid (such as dividing by zero or reading outside its own memory) or asks for anything not listed here is stopped, and the window says why. Findings reported before it stopped are kept.

The sandbox is strong, but a plug-in is still a program someone else wrote, and it sees the whole binary you open. Install plug-ins only from sources you trust, and be aware that its findings are only as good as its author's rules.

Writing a plug-in

Any language that compiles to WebAssembly works (Rust, C, Zig and others). The module must export a function named run that takes nothing and returns nothing or one i32, and may import only these functions from the module ocw:

FunctionMeaning
input_size() -> i64Size of the open binary in bytes
input_read(offset: i64, ptr: i32, len: i32) -> i32Copies up to len bytes starting at offset to memory address ptr; returns how many were copied
function_count() -> i32Number of functions found
function_address(index: i32) -> i64Address of function index
function_name(index: i32, ptr: i32, capacity: i32) -> i32Copies the name (UTF-8) to ptr, at most capacity bytes; returns the full length
report(severity: i32, address: i64, ptr: i32, len: i32)Adds a finding; severity 0 info, 1 low, 2 medium, 3 high. The address is the plug-in's choice: use a function address for findings about a function, or a position in the file for a finding about bytes (it is shown, and added to notes, as given)
log(ptr: i32, len: i32)Adds a line to the log

Compile for the basic WebAssembly feature set. With Rust, for example: rustc --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -C target-cpu=mvp -C opt-level=s -C panic=abort --crate-type cdylib -C link-arg=--export=run plugin.rs. The sandbox understands the original WebAssembly instructions plus sign extension, saturating conversions, bulk memory operations and multiple results; a module that uses anything else (vector instructions, threads, reference types) is refused with a message, as is a module that imports anything not in the table.

Open Archive

Binary > Open Archive... lists the files inside a zip, jar, apk, nupkg, whl, tar, tar.gz, tar.xz, tar.bz2, tar.zst, 7z, rar, cab, msi (Windows Installer packages), NSIS 3, Inno Setup 6.5+, WiX Burn bundles, single-volume InstallShield cabinets, ar (including Debian .deb packages and static libraries) or cpio archive, or a single file compressed with gzip, xz, bzip2 or zstd. Choose a file and Open selected in Binary Workbench. Unsafe entries (for example names that point outside the archive, links and zip entries that are suspiciously compressed) are flagged and cannot be opened; very large entries are refused. Nothing in an archive is run. RAR support covers the current RAR 5 format (as made by WinRAR 5 and later), including solid archives and large dictionaries, as well as stored (uncompressed) RAR 4 entries. A Windows Installer package (.msi) is listed under its real folders and file names (such as Program Files/Demo/readme.txt) and its files can be opened; the package is only read, never installed. A Cabinet (.cab) and the cabinet inside an msi can be stored, MSZIP-compressed or LZX-compressed; files compressed with Quantum, packages whose cabinet is a separate file that is not next to the msi, and multi-part cabinets are listed but marked as not supported. An NSIS installer (.exe) made by NSIS 3 is listed with the files it would install, under the folders its script sets (the installer is only read, never run); deflate, bzip2 and LZMA data is supported, solid or not, ANSI or Unicode. When an installer compresses each file separately, the sizes shown are the compressed sizes. An Inno Setup installer (.exe) of version 6.5 or later (checked against 6.7) is listed the same way, with its stored, zlib, bzip2, LZMA and LZMA2 data, solid or not, and the files are checked against the checksums the installer holds; installers that are password-protected or split over several disk files, and Inno Setup versions whose layout differs from the one checked, are refused with a message. Password-protected 7z and RAR archives, legacy compressed RAR 1.5–2.9 streams, archives split into several volumes, zstd files that need a dictionary, NSIS 2 and older, Inno Setup before 6.5 and multi-volume encrypted InstallShield setups are not supported; the window says so for the file concerned.

Damage report and archive salvage

When a captured sample, crash upload or archive is truncated or partially corrupted, choose Binary > Damage Report & Archive Salvage…. Proxalume scans the damaged ZIP, TAR, GZIP or executable container without failing on broken end-of-central-directory or header pointers, reports every structural defect and CRC mismatch it found, and lets you salvage intact member entries for inspection.

Open Memory Dump

Binary > Open Memory Dump... opens a Windows memory dump (a .dmp minidump, as written by Task Manager's "Create dump file", Windows Error Reporting, ProcDump or a debugger) and shows what it records. The dump is only read; nothing in it is run. The summary names the processor, the Windows version, the process ID and when the dump was written, and, for a crash dump, the exception and where it happened (the module and the offset inside it). The tabs list:

  • Modules: every program and library the process had loaded, with its address range and file version.
  • Threads: each thread, the address it was running at (and in which module) and its stack.
  • Memory map: every region of the address space with its state, protection and type, for dumps written with memory information. Executable memory that belongs to no module (for example injected or generated code) is worth a closer look.
  • Exception: the exception code, address, thread and parameters, when the dump records one.
  • Captured memory: the ranges whose contents the dump holds. Double-click a range, or type an address and choose Show bytes, to see the bytes there in hex.

A damaged or truncated dump still opens; what could not be read is listed as a warning. Kernel dumps (full and kernel memory dumps of the whole computer) are not supported. To preserve a minidump alongside Windows Prefetch, .lnk shortcuts and browser history timelines in an encrypted chain-of-custody bundle, see Forensic cases and OS artifact triage.

Find similar functions

With a function selected in the Functions tab, Binary > Find Similar Functions (this binary)... or (another file)... lists functions that look similar, with a likeness percentage. A high score means a similar shape, not proof of the same source; compare the two functions before drawing conclusions. Double-click a result in the same binary to jump to it.

Debugger (Windows 32 and 64-bit, Linux x86 and x86-64)

Binary > Debug Open Binary (runs it)... starts the open program under a debugger. This runs the program on your computer with your permissions, so you are asked to confirm and shown the file's SHA-256 first. Use it only for programs you trust.

It works for Windows programs (32-bit and 64-bit; a 32-bit program shows its 32-bit registers such as eip and esp) and, when the application runs on an x86-64 Linux computer, for x86 and x86-64 Linux programs. Programs started this way print into the log. Linux may restrict debugging in some setups (for example inside some containers); the log says so when it refuses.

  • Start runs the program and, by default, stops at its entry point. Continue, Step (one instruction) and Stop control it.
  • Breakpoints: enter an address as shown in the listing (hexadecimal), or use At selected function. Change breakpoints before starting or while stopped.
  • Registers and Memory (64 bytes at an address you choose) are shown while the program is stopped.
  • The program is ended when you click Stop, close the window or exit the application.

Limits: DLLs and shared libraries, macOS programs and Linux programs on ARM computers are not supported; only one thread is followed; there is no symbol or source information, no watchpoints, no thread list, no call stack view and no attaching to a running process. The debugger is not a sandbox: a malicious program can still do harm when it runs.

Not available

Graphical workflow editors, remote or conditional workflow steps, extensions that run unsandboxed host code or add menus, archive formats beyond those above (legacy compressed RAR 1.5–2.9 streams, Quantum-compressed cabinets, NSIS 2 and older, Inno Setup before 6.5 and multi-volume encrypted InstallShield setups), and fuzzy cross-binary matching beyond the likeness list.

Writing your own security rules

Analyze > Security Rule Editor... lets you write the extra vulnerability rules the scanner applies on top of its built-in checks.

  • A rule has an ID, a severity (Warning or Error), a language (or Any), a message that explains the finding, a pattern and an optional how to fix it note. The pattern is a regular expression and ignores capitals.
  • New rule adds one; Delete rule removes the selected one. Paste some code into Sample code to test on and choose Test on the sample to see which lines the pattern matches before you rely on it.
  • The editor refuses to save a rule that has no ID or message, a pattern that is not a valid regular expression, a pattern that matches empty text (it would flag every file), or an ID used twice.
  • Save writes the pack to a file and makes it the pack the scanner uses (the same box as Settings > Extra vulnerability rules file). The rules apply from the next scan. Open a pack... edits an existing file, and Save as... writes a copy.
  • A pattern that runs for more than two seconds on one file is stopped and skipped; the other rules still apply.

Test coverage

Analyze > Test Coverage... reads a coverage report that another tool wrote after running your tests, and shows how well each file of the open project is covered.

  • Supported reports: LCOV (.info), Cobertura XML, JaCoCo XML, Istanbul/nyc JSON (coverage-final.json) and coverage.py JSON. The format is recognised from the file.
  • Files are listed from least to best covered, with the number of lines covered. Select a file to see which lines no test reached. A filter box narrows the list.
  • The report's file paths are matched to your project's files by the end of the path, so a report made on another machine (with different folders) still lines up. Files in the report that are not in the open project are counted and the first is named.
  • Nothing is run: the application only reads the report. Open the project first.

License check

Analyze > License Check... screens the licences of the packages your project depends on, using the licence names recorded in your dependency files (npm, Composer and NuGet record them; other sources may not).

  1. Choose how your project is shared: sold or given out as a closed-source product, used only inside your organisation, published as open source under a permissive licence, or published as open source under GPL-3.0.
  2. Choose Scan dependencies and check. Every package is placed in a class (permissive, weak copyleft such as LGPL or MPL, strong copyleft such as GPL, network copyleft such as AGPL, non-commercial, source-available, or unknown) and given a verdict: Fine, Review or Conflict.
  3. Select a row for the reason. Copy report puts a table on the clipboard.

For a closed-source product, GPL, AGPL and non-commercial licences are conflicts, LGPL and MPL need review (how the library is linked matters), and anything missing or unrecognised is marked for review rather than assumed fine. OR lets you pick the better option and AND applies the stricter one. This is a first screening to find what to read, not legal advice.

Updates: checking for a newer version

Proxalume can tell you when a newer, signed version exists and install it for you using compact differential patches. Nothing is installed without your say-so: you are told that an update exists, and you choose Update now or leave it for later.

Check now

Choose Help > Check for Updates.... The window shows the installed version and, after a moment, one of these:

MessageMeaning
You have the latest version.Nothing newer is published for your channel.
Version X is available.A signed update exists. The release notes are shown. Update now downloads and installs it (see below); Remind me later closes the window; Skip this version stops offering that version.
Version X requires active maintenance.A newer release exists, but its publication date is after your saved license's maintenance window (see below). Your current installation continues to work without restriction.
The update information could not be retrieved.No connection, or the update address did not answer. Nothing was changed.
The update information was not signed by a trusted key and was ignored.The information could not be verified, so it was not used.
Update checking is not available in this build.Updates cannot be offered by this build.
This is a development build.Builds made from source never check on their own.

When a signed update is waiting, a small Update X available button also appears in the status bar.

Update now
