Update now does everything in one go: it downloads only the changed files (differential binary patches) when upgrading from a recent release, verifies every file's cryptographic hash and publisher signature, prepares the new version next to the current one, then closes the application, swaps the two and starts the new version. You do not download or copy anything yourself. A progress bar shows the download, and Cancel stops it at any time before the swap.

  • Your settings, projects, local license vault and saved work are not touched.
  • If the new version does not start properly, the previous version is put back automatically and the next start tells you that the update did not work. Nothing is lost.
  • If the installation folder is not writable (for example it is in a protected location), the window says so and nothing is changed. Move the application to a folder you can write to.
  • If your installed copy is too old to be patched incrementally, the window tells you to download the latest full package from your account downloads page.

License and maintenance eligibility

In commercially licensed builds, update installation is tied to your license's maintenance window (see License and activation):

  • Perpetual licenses include 12 months of updates from purchase. Every release published on or before your Maintenance through date is permanently covered.
  • When you click Update now, Proxalume checks that the new release's publication date is covered by your unlocked license and presents your license key over HTTPS (X-License-Key) to download the signed update payload.
  • If a new release is published after your maintenance date has passed, your installed perpetual version keeps working offline forever, and Update now explains that active maintenance is required. After renewing maintenance on the website, open Help > License and Activation… and choose Activate / refresh online to unlock the newer release.

Automatic checks

On the first start of an installed release the application asks once whether to check automatically. If you agree it checks at most once a day (a failed attempt also counts, so a broken address is not retried at every start), in the background, and stays silent if anything goes wrong. Builds made from source never check on their own. You can change this at any time in Help > Check for Updates... (Check for updates automatically). Until you answer, nothing is checked on its own.

Channel

stable (the default) offers only finished releases. beta is for early builds. Choose in the same window.

What is sent, and what is trusted

  • An availability check downloads two small files (the release description and its signature) over HTTPS. Only standard request details (your IP address and a user agent naming the application version) are visible to the server during a check; when downloading a commercial update package with Update now, your license key header is included to verify update maintenance eligibility. No project name, file path or analysis data is ever sent.
  • Only updates that carry a valid cryptographic signature from the publisher's embedded public key are offered or installed; anything else is rejected before touching your installation.

Command line

Proxalume --check-update prints the result and sets the exit code: 0 nothing newer, 1 a newer release exists, 2 the check could not be completed, or the update information could not be used (for example it was expired, not trusted or for another channel). Exit code 0 means no usable newer release was found. Proxalume --update does the same check and, when a newer signed release exists, installs it without a window (exit code 2 if it could not be done). Exit code 0 means nothing was needed or the installation was started; the swap itself finishes after the command ends, and if the new version does not start the previous one is restored and the next start reports it. The command refuses to run while another copy of the application is running from the same folder.

Not available

Updating copies that have been modified on disk or whose baseline version is no longer in the differential patch archive: download a fresh full archive from the website Downloads page instead (your settings and license vault in %APPDATA%/Proxalume carry over automatically).

Binary Workbench

Binary Workbench: opening a file safely

A binary is a compiled program or library: a Windows .exe or .dll, a Linux executable or .so, a macOS executable or .dylib, or a firmware image. The Binary Workbench lets you look inside one: what it is made of, what text it contains, what functions it has and how the code flows.

Inspecting is not running

Important Opening a binary in the Workbench does not execute it. The file is read as data, hashed, parsed and disassembled (turned into readable instruction text). Nothing in it runs.

Running or debugging an untrusted program is a different activity with real risk: malware can damage files, steal data or spread. The Workbench itself never runs a program; the separate debugger does so only when you start it and confirm. If you later decide to run a suspicious program, do it only in an isolated virtual machine that you are prepared to discard.

Still follow common sense with unknown files: keep them in a dedicated folder, do not double-click them in your file manager, and keep your operating system and security software up to date. Patching (see Annotating, patching and the hex editor) edits the file you opened, so work on a copy.

Open a binary

  1. Choose Binary > Open Binary…, press Ctrl+B, or use Open Binary… at the top of the Binary Workbench tab.
  2. Select the file. Analysis starts straight away in the background; the window stays responsive and a status message shows progress. Opening another file cancels the analysis in progress.
  3. The Workbench shows nine sub-tabs: Triage, Functions & CFG, Strings, Imports & Symbols, Compare, Overview, Session & Hex, Types and Pseudo-C. You can also jump to most of them from the Binary menu.

Keep several binaries open

Opening another file does not close the previous one. When more than one binary is open, an Open binaries list appears above the tabs: choose a name to switch to it, and the analysis you already did comes back at once. Close this binary removes the one you are looking at. Up to eight binaries stay open; opening a ninth closes the one that has been open the longest. Opening the same file again refreshes its entry instead of adding a second one.

Function names from debug information

If the program has debug information, the Workbench uses it automatically:

  • Windows programs: a PDB file next to the program (same folder, same name with .pdb, or the file name the program was built with) is read, but only when it matches that exact build. A PDB that belongs to a different build is reported and ignored. Functions found there are named (for example Widget::Method) and also help the analysis find code. The PDB's structure layouts (classes and structs with their member offsets) are read too.
  • Linux programs: names and addresses of functions are read from the DWARF information inside the file when it was built with -g.

The Types tab says what was found and can import structure layouts from DWARF or from a matching PDB. A layout is left out when it cannot be shown exactly (bit fields, virtual base classes, pointers to members); a union is shown as raw bytes, and names such as std::vector<int> are written with underscores (std_vector_int). Compressed DWARF sections are not supported.

Identify the format and architecture

The Overview and Triage tabs show the detected format (PE for Windows, ELF for Linux, Mach-O for macOS, or .NET metadata when present), the CPU architecture (for example x64 or ARM64), the entry point and sections. If the format is not recognized, you will see a clear message and the file can still be examined as raw bytes.

Open a firmware or shellcode image (no headers)

Some files, such as a flash dump from a microcontroller, have no header that says what CPU they are for. For those:

  1. Choose Binary > Open Raw / Firmware Image… (or Open Raw… in the tab).
  2. Select the file. A small dialog opens.
  3. Choose the Architecture (for example thumb (Thumb-2, little-endian) for a Cortex-M chip), the Base address the image is loaded at (hex, such as 0x08000000) and optionally an Entry point offset.
  4. For ARM Cortex-M firmware, tick Cortex-M: read the vector table to find the reset handler and interrupt handlers automatically.
  5. Click Analyze.

A wrong architecture or base address produces meaningless disassembly (garbage instructions or no functions). If that happens, re-open the image with different settings. A raw image has no symbols, imports or section names, so there is less to see.

What is supported

See What the Binary Workbench supports for the full list of formats and architectures and how well each has been verified.

Next: Triage, headers, sections and entropy.

Triage, headers, sections and entropy

Triage is a first look: "what is this file, is it unusual, and where should I look next?" It is the first sub-tab after you open a binary.

What the Triage tab shows

  • Hashes. The file's MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256 digests (SHA-256 is the one to rely on; MD5 and SHA-1 are shown only because other tools still quote them). A hash is a fingerprint of the file's exact bytes: if one byte changes, the hash changes. Use it to confirm you have the same file as someone else, or to look the file up elsewhere. A hash identifies contents; it does not tell you who made the file or whether it is safe.
  • Entropy graph. Entropy measures how random the bytes are, from 0 (all the same) to 8 bits per byte (random). Ordinary code and text sit well below 8. Compressed or encrypted data sits near 8. A section or region near 8 may be packed, compressed or encrypted, which is a reason to look closer, not proof of malware (many legitimate files contain compressed data). Click the graph to jump to that part of the file.
  • Sections with their size in the file and entropy. A section is a named region such as the code (.text) or data (.data). Segments (in ELF and Mach-O) are the regions the operating system maps into memory.
  • Notable strings. Text found in the file that looks interesting: URLs, IP addresses, file paths, registry keys, email addresses and debug (PDB) paths. Select one to see where it is used.
  • Header information: entry point, image base and the other summary values on the Overview tab.
Note The notable-strings list is heuristic. It filters out some short random-looking text, so it can miss real strings and include harmless ones. Use the full Strings tab for everything.

File offsets and virtual addresses

Two kinds of location appear throughout the Workbench:

  • A file offset is a position counted from the first byte of the file on disk.
  • A virtual address (VA) is where that byte sits in memory when the program is loaded. Disassembly and functions are shown by virtual address, because that is what the program itself uses. An RVA (relative virtual address, used by Windows files) is a VA measured from the image base.

The two differ because the operating system spreads sections out when loading them. The Workbench converts between them for you: the Strings tab shows both the offset and the address, and Go to address (Ctrl+G) takes a virtual address in hexadecimal.

Entry point

The entry point is the address where execution would begin. It is shown in the Overview. It is often not the program's main function, but startup code that eventually calls it.

Next

Look at the code itself: Functions, disassembly, control-flow graphs and cross-references.

Functions, disassembly, control-flow graphs and cross-references

Open the Functions & CFG sub-tab (or Binary > Functions and Control-Flow Graph).

Disassembly and pseudo-code

Disassembly shows the machine instructions in a readable form, such as mov eax, 1 or call 0x401000. Decompilation turns them back into something like C source. The Pseudo-C sub-tab does that for the function selected in the function list, for x86, x86-64, 64-bit ARM (AArch64) 32-bit ARM (ARM state and Thumb-2), RISC-V, 32-bit PowerPC and 32-bit MIPS code (other architectures show a message instead).

What to expect: registers become variables (rax, rcx...), stack slots become locals (local_10), comparisons are folded into conditions, and loops and if/else are rebuilt where the control flow allows (anything else keeps a goto and a label). Every value is an unsigned integer of its machine width, with explicit casts where the machine code treats it as signed. Parameters are the registers the function reads before writing (in the calling convention's order) and its stack arguments; the function returns rax when it sets it. Names of called functions come from the symbols, imports and your own renames. The arguments of a call are guessed from the registers (or pushed values) set just before it, so a call can show fewer arguments than the function really takes.

String scans and compares (scas, cmps, with or without rep) are shown as a call that returns how many elements it went through, with a small helper function written at the top; the flags after a repeated one assume at least one element was compared.

It also handles add-with-carry and subtract-with-borrow, bit tests, block fills and copies (shown as memset and a loop of memmove calls), SSE register moves and bit operations, addresses of stack arrays, and jumps through a table (shown as a switch whose cases jump to labels).

64-bit ARM: the variables are the registers x0...x30 (a 32-bit w register is shown as the low half of its x register), the first eight arguments are x0...x7, the function returns x0, and stack arguments are arg_0, arg_8 and so on. The integer instruction set is covered: moves, add and subtract (with flags and carry), logic, shifts, bit-field moves, multiply, divide, conditional select, every load and store form including pairs, and branches (including jumps through a table). Dividing by zero gives 0, as on the processor. Saving and restoring the registers a function must preserve is left out of the result. Floating-point and vector (NEON) instructions, atomic and exclusive loads and stores, and pointer-authentication or other system instructions appear as comments. A call through a register is shown as __ocw_icall(target, arguments...), with a one-line #define at the top that turns it into a normal C call. Dividing the most negative number by -1 gives the dividend negated, as on the processor.

32-bit ARM: code in ARM state and in Thumb-2 (with its IT blocks) is translated. The variables are the registers r0...r12 and lr, the first four arguments are r0...r3, the function returns r0, and stack arguments are arg_0, arg_4 and so on. The integer instruction set compilers use is covered: data processing with every operand form (shifts by 32 or more give the processor's result), multiply and the 64-bit multiplies, word, byte, halfword and signed loads and stores in every addressing mode, constants loaded from the code, push, pop, ldm and stm, extends, movw and movt, branches, calls and returns. A conditionally executed instruction becomes a conditional assignment, or moves onto the branch it belongs to, and a conditional return becomes a branch to a return. Calls to the run-time division helpers are written as division. Recognized, bounds-checked jump tables are shown as switches. Unrecognized computed jumps, floating-point and vector instructions remain comments.

RISC-V: 32-bit and 64-bit code is translated (RV32 and RV64), including the compressed instructions. The variables are the registers x0...x31, the first eight arguments are x10...x17 (a0...a7), the function returns x10, and stack arguments are arg_0, arg_8 and so on. The base integer instructions, multiply and divide (dividing by zero and the one overflowing division give the processor's result), the address and basic bit-manipulation extensions (Zba, Zbb) and conditional zeroing (Zicond) are covered, with loads and stores, branches, calls, tail calls and returns. Bounds-checked jump tables are shown as switches. Floating-point, vector, atomic and system instructions remain comments.

32-bit PowerPC: big-endian 32-bit code is translated. The variables are the registers r0...r31 and ctr, the first eight arguments are r3...r10, the function returns r3, and stack arguments are arg_8, arg_C and so on. The integer instructions compilers use are covered: arithmetic with the carry bit, logic, shifts (by 32 or more giving the processor's result) and the rotate-and-mask instructions, compares into any condition field and the branches that test them, loops counted down in ctr, loads and stores in every form, calls, tail calls and conditional returns, and the register save and restore routines -Os code calls. Division by zero, which the processor leaves undefined, gives 0. Bounds-checked jump tables are shown as switches. A stack variable read or written in part (a byte of a word) takes the bytes the program's byte order names. Other memory is read and written in the program's own byte order, so code that reads a value back at another size than it was written with means what it does on the processor only on a big-endian machine. Floating-point, vector and system instructions remain comments; 64-bit PowerPC shows a message.

32-bit MIPS: 32-bit code in either byte order is translated (the o32 convention). The variables are the registers r0...r31 with hi and lo, the first four arguments are r4...r7, the function returns r2, and stack arguments are arg_10, arg_14 and so on. Each branch's delay slot (the instruction after it, which runs before the branch takes effect) is placed where it runs. The integer instructions compilers use are covered: arithmetic, logic, shifts and rotates, compares, conditional moves, multiply and divide through hi and lo, the bit-field and extend instructions of MIPS32 release 2, loads and stores, branches, calls, tail calls and returns. The divide-by-zero checks compilers add (teq) become a branch to a trap, and dividing by zero, which the processor leaves undefined, gives 0. Bounds-checked jump tables are shown as switches. Values reached through the global pointer (gp), floating-point, unaligned, atomic and system instructions remain comments; 64-bit MIPS shows a message.

Limits: it is a reading aid, not the original source. Types, structures, arrays, strings and variable names are not recovered. Instructions it cannot translate (floating-point arithmetic and other vector instructions, jumps through tables it does not recognise, thread-local access, direct changes to the stack pointer) appear as comments and the status line says how many; a function that uses them is only a best effort. For the functions it fully translates, the pseudo-code is valid C that computes the same result as the machine code. Always check important findings against the disassembly.

Likewise the application analyzes static files by default; the separate debugger runs programs only when you ask it to.

The function list

On the left is Discovered functions. The application finds functions by following the program from its entry point, exports and symbols, following direct calls, and reading the compiler's own tables (such as Windows .pdata and ELF .eh_frame_hdr). Each function shows its address, name and the evidence and confidence for it (for example "from symbol", "from direct call").

  • Type in Filter functions by name or address to narrow the list.
  • Select a function to show its disassembly, its control-flow graph, its callers and its callees.

Functions with no symbols are named from their address (sub_…). Functions that only jump to an imported function are named after that import.

Limitation Code that is reached only through indirect calls the analyzer cannot resolve (for example some virtual-method tables and callbacks) is found only if the file's tables list it. Each analyzed binary reports how much of its code it decoded.

Go to an address

Press Ctrl+G (or Binary > Go to Address…), type a hexadecimal virtual address such as 401000, and press Go. If an address is not inside a known function, you are told so.

Callers and callees (cross-references)

A cross-reference (xref) says "this place refers to that place". For the selected function:

  • Callers (xrefs to) lists the places that call it.
  • Callees (xrefs from) lists what it calls.

Select an entry to jump there. Direct calls, jumps, references to data and strings (for x86/x64 and ARM64), imports and resolved switch tables are covered. Calls through values computed at run time are not.

The control-flow graph

A basic block is a run of instructions with one way in at the top and one way out at the end. The control-flow graph (CFG) draws each block as a box and each possible jump as an arrow. It is the quickest way to see loops and if branches.

  • Click a block to select its address. The Selected address line then feeds annotating and patching.
  • Use +, − and 100% to zoom. Binary > Zoom CFG In and Binary > Zoom CFG Out do the same.
  • Arrows leaving a function are drawn to a stub. Arrows that go back up (loops) run along the right edge.
  • Highlighted blocks (see Annotating) are filled with your chosen color; the color is also named in the annotation list.

Strings, imports and exports

  • Strings sub-tab: every string found, with its file offset, address and section. Type in Filter strings. Select a string to see Referenced from locations and click one to jump to the code that uses it.
  • Imports & Symbols sub-tab: the functions the file imports from libraries (what it asks the operating system to do), the functions it exports, and symbols. Type in Filter imports, exports and symbols.

Reading imports is a quick way to guess behavior: a program importing networking, file and process-creation functions does those kinds of things, though imports alone do not prove what it does with them.

Switch statements

Compilers often turn a switch into a table of jump targets. The analyzer recognizes common patterns on x86/x64 and ARM64 and draws the branches. Unusual or unbounded tables are left unresolved rather than guessed.

Next: Annotating, patching and the hex editor.

Annotating, patching and the hex editor

Annotate what you learn

In Functions & CFG, the Annotate section (expand it if it is collapsed) records your findings so you do not have to remember them. Annotations are stored in your user profile, keyed by the file's SHA-256 hash, so they come back whenever you open the same file again, wherever it is. If the file changes, its hash changes and it is treated as a new file.

  1. Click a block in the CFG, or use Go to address, so that an address is selected (the Selected address line shows it).
  2. Choose what to record:
  3. Rename selected function - type a name in Function name, then click the button. The new name appears everywhere.
  4. Save comment - type in Comment at selected address.
  5. Add tag - a label such as crypto or suspicious.
  6. Bookmark - toggles a bookmark at the address.
  7. Highlight - choose a color in the Highlight colour box, then click Highlight. Choose Clear highlight to remove it. Highlighted blocks are filled with that color in the CFG.
  8. All of them are listed under Your annotations. Select one and click Remove selected annotation to delete it.

The Binary menu also has Rename Function and Toggle Bookmark.

Patch a binary

Warning Patching changes the file on disk. Always work on a copy of the original. A patched program may crash or behave unpredictably. Patch only files you are allowed to modify, and only for lawful purposes such as testing, repair and research.

Open the Patch section (collapsed by default).

  1. Select the address of the instruction (click its block, or Go to address).
  2. Choose a patch type: NOP out instruction, Invert conditional jump, Always jump, Never jump, Return immediately, Write raw bytes or Assemble instructions (x86/x64/ARM/ARM64/MIPS/PowerPC/RISC-V). The first five are provided for x86/x64 and ARM64 files; on other architectures use Write raw bytes.
  3. Click Preview. The status shows the original bytes, the new bytes and the exact instruction text. Nothing is written yet.
  4. If it looks right, click Apply to file.
  5. To undo, click Revert last.

How the safeguards work:

  • Verification before writing. The bytes currently in the file must match what the preview expected. If the file changed on disk in the meantime, the patch is refused with a message that the file changed.
  • Backup. The first time you patch a file, a copy is saved next to it with .bak added to its name (for example app.exe.bak). It is never overwritten by later patches. Keep it.
  • Atomic write. The new file is written to a temporary file and swapped in, so a failure cannot leave a half-written file.
  • Recorded and revertible. Each patch is logged with its address, the original and new bytes, and the time; Revert last restores the original bytes (again only if the bytes still match).
  • Re-analysis. After a patch or revert, the file is analyzed again. Your annotations are carried over to the file's new hash.
Typing assembly

Choose Assemble instructions (x86/x64/ARM/ARM64/MIPS/PowerPC/RISC-V) and type the new code in the text box, one instruction per line or separated by ;, for example xor eax, eax then ret. Registers, numbers (0x28, 28h or plain decimal) and memory operands such as [rbp-4], dword ptr [rbx+rcx*4+8] are understood, and branches take an absolute address (jmp 0x140001020, call 140002000). db 90, CC writes raw bytes. A line such as loop: defines a label that branches can name (jnz loop), and .equ NAME, 0x10 defines a constant that later lines can use. Other directives and macros are not supported.

64-bit ARM (AArch64) code is assembled by the same box: moves, add and subtract, logic, shifts, multiply and divide, conditional select, loads and stores (single, pair, offset, pre-index, post-index and register offset), adr/adrp, and the branches (b, bl, b.eq and the other conditions, cbz, cbnz, tbz, tbnz, br, blr, ret), plus nop, svc, brk and .word. Every instruction is four bytes, so the new instructions replace exactly that many existing ones and nothing is padded. Labels and .equ work the same way (cbnz x0, loop). For AArch64, floating-point, vector and system instructions are not supported by the assembler (use Write raw bytes). RISC-V code (32-bit or 64-bit) is assembled too: the integer instructions (loads and stores, arithmetic, logic, shifts, lui, auipc, branches, jal, jalr), multiply and divide, the atomic instructions (lr, sc, amo*), fence, ecall, ebreak, the CSR instructions, and the usual shorthand (nop, mv, li for 32-bit values, not, neg, j, jr, ret, beqz and its relatives). RISC-V programs often use 2-byte compressed instructions, so the new code replaces whole existing instructions of either length and the remainder is filled with NOPs; give the address of an instruction as the disassembly shows it, because RISC-V has no way to tell from the bytes alone where an instruction starts. The assembler writes 4-byte instructions only; floating-point, vector and compressed instructions are not supported by it. MIPS code (32-bit or 64-bit, big or little endian, as the program is) is assembled as well: the integer instructions (arithmetic, logic, shifts and rotates, multiply and divide, hi/lo moves, loads and stores including the unaligned and linked forms, branches, j, jal, jr, jalr), the 64-bit forms (ld, sd, daddu, dsll and the rest) for 64-bit programs, a few system instructions (syscall, break, sync, eret, mfc0, mtc0) and the usual shorthand (nop, move, li for 32-bit values, b, beqz, bnez, negu, not). Registers are written $4, $a0 or $sp (in 64-bit programs $a4 to $a7 are registers 8 to 11 and $t0 to $t3 are 12 to 15, as in the 64-bit ABIs); the 64-bit instructions are accepted in any program, because the n32 ABI uses them in 32-bit files. Lines such as .set noreorder are accepted and ignored. Every instruction is four bytes and replaces one existing word each; the shorthand li with a value that needs both halves takes two words. Nothing is reordered for you: the instruction after a branch or jump is its delay slot, so write a nop there if you want it empty. Floating-point and other coprocessor instructions are not supported by the assembler. PowerPC code (32-bit or 64-bit, big or little endian, as the program is) is assembled too: the integer instructions (add and subtract with their carry and overflow forms, multiply and divide, logic, shifts and rotates including rlwinm and the 64-bit rld forms, compares, loads and stores with an offset or an index register, lwarx and stwcx.), branches (b, bl, bc, blr, bctr and the conditional shorthands such as beq, bne cr1, target, bdnz), the special-register moves (mflr, mtctr, mfspr and so on), sc, tw, sync, isync, and the usual shorthand (nop, li, lis, mr, not, sub, slwi, srwi, clrlwi, sldi, srdi). Registers are written r3 (or just 3) and compare fields cr0 to cr7. Every instruction is four bytes and replaces exactly one existing word. Floating-point and vector instructions and branch-prediction hints (beq+) are not supported by the assembler. 32-bit ARM code is assembled as well, in ARM state or Thumb-2, in the unified syntax (adds r0, r1, #1, addseq, ldrbeq: the s and the size come before the condition): data processing with immediates, shifted registers and register-specified shifts, movw/movt, multiply and divide, clz, byte reversal, sign and zero extension, bit-field instructions, loads and stores (word, byte, halfword, signed, double and exclusive, with offset, pre-index and post-index), ldm/stm/push/pop, b, bl, bx, blx, adr, svc, bkpt, mrs/msr, barriers and hints. As the GNU assembler does, an immediate that does not fit is written the opposite way where there is one (add r0, r1, #-1 becomes sub r0, r1, #1; mov becomes movw or mvn). The application uses the instruction set the analysis found for the code at that address (ARM or Thumb); where no analyzed function covers the address, put .arm or .thumb on the first line to say which it is. Big-endian ARM programs are not supported, because the byte order of their instructions depends on how they were linked. Thumb-2 is assembled in the unified syntax, choosing the 16-bit form of an instruction whenever there is one, as the GNU assembler does (adds r0, r1, #1 is 2 bytes, add r0, r1, #1 is 4; .n and .w force one or the other). Conditional instructions must sit inside an it block, as the hardware requires, and a branch to a label uses the short form when it reaches. Thumb instructions are 2 or 4 bytes, so the new code replaces whole existing instructions and the rest is filled with 16-bit NOPs; give the address of an instruction as the disassembly shows it, and do not start a patch in the middle of an it block. Literal pools, floating-point and NEON are not supported. In ARM state every instruction is four bytes and replaces exactly one existing word. Loading a constant with = needs a literal pool and is not supported; floating-point and NEON instructions are not supported either.

The new code replaces whole instructions: if it is shorter than the instructions it covers, the rest is filled with NOP so the code after it stays where it was. Preview shows exactly which instructions are replaced and the bytes that will be written. A mistake (an unknown instruction, operands that do not fit) is explained in the status line and nothing is written.

Structure layouts (the Types tab)

The Types tab shows what the bytes at an address mean when read as a structure you describe. Write layouts the way C declares them:

struct Header {
    uint32 magic;
    uint16 version;
    char   name[8];
    ptr    next;
}

Types are int8 uint8 int16 uint16 int32 uint32 int64 uint64 float double char bool and ptr (the pointer size of the binary), arrays like name[8], and other layouts from the same text. Fields are packed one after another; write struct Name align { ... } to pad each field to its natural alignment like a C compiler. Choose a layout, type an address in hexadecimal (or a file offset such as f:0x40), optionally tick Big-endian, and click Read here. Each field is listed with its offset, type and value. Reading never changes the file, and your layouts are saved with the binary. Use selected address copies the address you selected in the Functions tab. When the program has DWARF debug information, Import structures from debug info adds its structures to your text.

Sharing your notes

Binary > Export My Notes... writes your function names, comments, tags, bookmarks, highlights and structure layouts to a file. Someone who has the same binary can open it and choose Binary > Import Shared Notes... to add them to theirs. The file records the fingerprint (SHA-256) of the binary, and the import refuses notes made for a different file. If both of you wrote something different at the same place, you are asked whether to keep your own notes or use the shared ones; items that do not clash are always added. Importing the same file twice changes nothing. The patch log is not shared, because it describes changes made on one computer. The file is plain text you can read before sending it; nothing in it is ever run.

The Hex Editor tab

View > Hex Editor (the tab with the numbers icon) edits any file inside the opened project folder as hexadecimal text. It is separate from the Binary Workbench and is intended for small corrections.

  1. In the Repository Explorer on the left, select a file.
  2. Click Load Selected File. Up to the first 32 KB is shown for editing; the status line says if the file is larger. The rest of the file is preserved when you save.
  3. Edit the hex bytes. Click Undo Last Edit to step back.
  4. Click Save Hex to write the file.

Safeguards:

  • The save is refused if the text is not valid hexadecimal, if the file no longer exists, if there was no checksum from loading, or if the file changed on disk since you loaded it. Reload, then redo your edit.
  • A .bak backup is made on the first save.
  • Writes are atomic, as above, and only files inside the project folder can be edited.

Next: Comparing binaries, sessions, reports and the command line.

Comparing binaries, sessions, reports and the command line

Compare two versions of a binary

Use this to see what changed between, for example, version 1 and version 2 of a program.

  1. Open the newer (or current) binary.
  2. Choose Binary > Compare With… (or Compare With… in the tab) and select the other file.
  3. Open the Compare sub-tab. Functions are listed as Changed, Added or Removed. Use the filter (All differences, Changed, Added, Removed) to narrow the list.

The comparison matches functions by their instruction patterns, so renamed or moved functions are usually still matched. It compares functions, not individual bytes or blocks, and it does not copy your annotations from one version to the other.

Sessions

A session remembers which binary you were investigating. In Session & Hex:

  • Save Binary Session stores the current binary's path and analysis summary.
  • Load Selected Session or Load Latest Session reopens it. If the stored file has moved or been deleted, you are told.
  • Compare Binary Baseline compares the current binary with a stored baseline summary.

Annotations are not part of a session; they are saved automatically per file hash (see Annotating).

Export a report

Binary > Export Report (JSON)… (or the button in the tab) writes a versioned JSON report of the analysis: hashes, sections, functions, calls, strings, imports and warnings. Use it to share results or to process them with scripts. Review it before sharing: it contains file names, paths and strings extracted from the file, which can include sensitive text.

Command line and automation

The same analysis can run without opening a window. Replace the paths with your own.

Proxalume --binary path/to/program.exe --out report.json
Proxalume --raw firmware.bin --arch thumb --base 0x08000000 --cortex-m --out report.json
Proxalume --binary-batch path/to/folder --out path/to/reports
Proxalume --binary-diff old.exe new.exe
  • --binary-batch writes one JSON report per file plus an index.json.
  • --selfcheck quickly verifies that the installed package works (it decodes a small program for each supported architecture and checks that the built-in guide is intact).
  • --mcp starts a local Model Context Protocol server over standard input/output so an AI tool can query a binary's functions and strings and add names or comments. It does not patch files. It has been tested at the protocol level; compatibility with every MCP client is not guaranteed.

On Windows, the executable is Proxalume.exe; on Linux, ./Proxalume.

Next: What the Binary Workbench supports.

Forensic cases and OS artifact triage

Proxalume includes a read-only digital forensics and incident response workbench for preserving suspect files, recording a cryptographic chain of custody, triaging operating-system execution artifacts and packaging portable .proxcase evidence bundles.

Important Every forensic acquisition and triage step is strictly read-only. Suspect binaries, memory dumps, shortcuts, Prefetch traces and browser databases are parsed as inert bytes and are never executed or modified on disk.

Creating or opening a forensic case

  • Choose Binary > New Forensic Case… to start an investigation with a fresh case ID, investigator label, classification and creation timestamp.
  • Choose Binary > Open Forensic Case… to open an existing .proxcase container (entering its password if the container was encrypted when exported).

The Forensic Case window organizes an investigation into four tabs: Evidence Artifacts, Chain of Custody, Correlated Timeline and Case Report.

Acquiring evidence and verifying cryptographic hashes

On the Evidence Artifacts tab:

  1. Choose Acquire Evidence File… and select a suspect executable, library, script, memory dump or operating-system artifact (up to 50 MB per interactive file).
  2. Proxalume reads the file once into memory, computes simultaneous SHA-256, SHA-1 and MD5 digests, records the file size and UTC timestamps, and appends a timestamped acquisition entry to the case's chain of custody.
  3. At any point during an investigation—or immediately after opening a .proxcase bundle from another analyst—choose Verify All Cryptographic Hashes. Proxalume re-computes every preserved payload's SHA-256, SHA-1 and MD5 digests against the recorded manifest, flags any mismatch immediately and logs the verification event in the custody ledger.

Automated OS artifact and memory dump triage

When you acquire supported forensic artifacts into a case, Proxalume automatically extracts structured execution evidence and correlates timestamps onto the Correlated Timeline tab:

Artifact typeWhat Proxalume extracts
Windows Shell Links (.lnk)Target executable path, command-line arguments, working directory, volume serial number, MAC timestamps and suspicious launcher indicators (for example hidden PowerShell or script hosts).
Windows Prefetch files (.pf)Decompresses Windows 10 and Windows 11 MAM Prefetch streams as well as uncompressed Windows 7/8 Prefetch files, recovering the executed binary name, Prefetch hash, run count, up to 8 last-execution timestamps and referenced module/file paths.
Browser history databases (SQLite)Parses Chromium (Chrome, Edge, Brave) urls/visits tables and Mozilla Firefox moz_places/moz_historyvisits tables in immutable read-only mode, converting WebKit and PRTime timestamps to UTC and flagging suspicious download or payload URLs.
Windows Minidumps (.dmp)Inspects process modules, thread contexts, exception records and memory protection descriptors, highlighting PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE (RWX) regions and unbacked executable memory ranges that may indicate code injection or shellcode. (For interactive hex inspection of captured memory ranges, see Open Memory Dump.)
Executables and libraries (.exe, .dll, ELF, Mach-O)Preserves multi-hash identity alongside static binary triage indicators; open the file in the Binary Workbench for full disassembly, control-flow graphs and pseudo-code.

Chain of custody and incident timeline

  • Chain of Custody: Lists every chronological action taken in the case—case creation, each artifact acquisition with its SHA-256 digest, integrity re-verifications and container exports—so reviewers can audit how evidence was handled.
  • Correlated Timeline: Merges file timestamps, Prefetch execution times, .lnk target timestamps, browser visit times and minidump capture times into a single UTC-sorted sequence, calling out anomalies and high-risk indicators.

Exporting .proxcase containers and Markdown reports

  • Markdown incident report: Switch to the Case Report tab to review a structured Markdown summary containing case metadata, the complete multi-hash evidence table, correlated timeline highlights and the full chain-of-custody log. Choose Copy Report Markdown to copy it to the clipboard for an incident ticket or report.
  • Portable .proxcase bundle: On the Evidence Artifacts tab, optionally enter a passphrase in Optional export password (AES-256-GCM) and choose Export Case (.proxcase)…. - When a password is supplied, the entire container is encrypted with AES-256-GCM using a key derived via PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 so sensitive samples and incident timelines can be transferred safely. - Exported .proxcase manifests automatically strip local analyst workstation folder paths (SourcePath), preserving only the artifact's original file name, hashes and bytes so your own machine's directory structure is never leaked when sharing a case.

Limits

Interactive acquisition in the Forensic Case window caps individual files at 50 MB to keep encrypted .proxcase bundles responsive. Full-machine disk images (.E01, raw multi-gigabyte disk volumes), full Windows kernel memory dumps, encrypted browser cookie values and live volatile memory capture from a running system are not supported; acquire individual triage files first with your collection tool of choice.

What the Binary Workbench supports (and does not)

Treat output for any file as a very good aid, not as ground truth. Support differs by format and processor, as listed below.

File formats

FormatSupport
Windows programs and libraries (.exe, .dll)Headers, sections, imports, exports and functions
Linux programs and libraries (32/64-bit, either byte order)Headers, sections, symbols and functions
macOS programs and librariesHeaders, sections, symbols and functions. Only the first part of a universal file is analyzed
.NET assembliesA summary only; the .NET code itself is not disassembled
Raw / firmware imagesYou supply the architecture and base address
Other containers (Intel HEX, S-record, UEFI images, ...)Not supported; convert to a raw image first

Processor architectures

ArchitectureStatus
x86 and x64Tested, including real files
ARM64 and 32-bit ARMTested, including real libraries. The newest vector instructions are shown as raw data
MIPS, PowerPC and RISC-VTested on generated test files only; not verified on real programs
Others (SPARC, m68k, MSP430...)Not supported. The Workbench says so rather than guessing

Capabilities that do not exist

  • Pseudo-code is supported for x86, x86-64, 64-bit ARM (AArch64), 32-bit ARM (ARM state and Thumb-2), RISC-V, 32-bit PowerPC and 32-bit MIPS (64-bit PowerPC and MIPS show a message). Pointer, array, structure-array and PDB/user structure layouts as well as SSE/SSE2, AVX/AVX2/AVX-512/FMA3 and 64/128-bit AArch64 NEON packed arithmetic, compares, broadcasts and shifts are translated, whereas masked EVEX opmasks, cross-lane vector shuffles and vector instructions on 32-bit ARM, RISC-V, PowerPC and MIPS are not.
  • Debugging only for Windows (32 and 64-bit) and Linux (x86 and x86-64) programs; not macOS, not ARM.
  • Plug-ins are sandboxed WebAssembly programs that can read the open binary and report findings. They cannot change it, read other files or use the network.
  • Struct layouts come from DWARF, a matching PDB or user-defined types. Layouts with bit fields or virtual base classes are left out, and at most 500 structures (plus the ones they use) are imported.
  • Assembly-text patching is for x86, x64, ARM (ARM state and Thumb-2), 64-bit ARM, MIPS, PowerPC and RISC-V only. Labels and .equ constants are accepted; macros are not.
  • Annotations are shared as files or synchronized over a shared folder (Binary > Live Shared Notes Sync…); there is no hosted internet collaboration server.

Anything not listed here should be assumed unsupported until tested.

When disassembly looks wrong

See Troubleshooting.

Settings and sharing

Settings, themes and preferences

Every preference in the application lives in one Settings window. Settings are global: they apply to every project, not to one project, and they are saved in a single file for your user.

Opening the Settings window

Choose Edit > Settings, click the ⚙ Settings toolbar button, press Ctrl+K and type settings, or open it from here. The window stays open beside the main window, so you can watch a change take effect.

  • Topics are listed on the left. Click one to see its settings.
  • Search (Ctrl+F inside the window) finds a setting by what it does, not where it lives. Try dark, font size, ignore, update, privacy or editor. Esc clears the search.
  • Changes are saved the moment you make them. There is no Apply button. Text boxes save when you press Enter or click somewhere else.
  • Each setting says when it takes effect: immediately, on the next scan (use File > Rescan or the Rescan now button that appears), the next time you open a binary, or the next time the application starts.
  • A setting that differs from its default shows Reset to default. Reset this page and Reset all settings put whole groups back. Resetting never touches your recent projects, suppressed findings or files.
  • A setting that cannot work as typed (for example an address without https://) shows a red message and is not saved until it is fixed.

Appearance

SettingWhat it does
Colour themeLight, Dark, or System, which follows your operating system's light or dark setting and changes when it does. The Dark theme is dark everywhere, including the graph, the 3D city and the control-flow views.
Interface size80% to 200%. Scales all text, buttons and panels together. Use a larger size if text is hard to read.
Show the Explorer / Inspector panelThe side panels. Also available under View > Panels.

Edit > Toggle Theme (Ctrl+T) flips between Light and Dark at any time.

Startup

  • Reopen my last project - opens the most recent project when the application starts.
  • View shown at start - which view is in front at start.
  • Recent projects to remember - how many File > Open Recent lists (0 to 50).

Project scanning

These control what is read and how when you open a project. They apply to the next scan.

SettingWhat it does
Files analyzed at onceMore is faster but uses more memory. 0 lets the application choose.
Deep (semantic) analysisCompiler-level analysis for languages that support it. Turn off for speed on very large projects.
Respect .gitignoreLeaves out what the project's own .gitignore files (and .git/info/exclude) ignore, following Git's own rules: *, ?, **, [ranges], ! to re-include, a trailing / for folders, and a leading / to anchor to the folder holding the file.
Skip common build and package foldersbin, obj, node_modules, vendor, dist, build, target and similar. The .git folder is always skipped.
Other folders and files to leave outOne name or folder path per line.
Extra folders to includeOther folders merged into the same analysis, one full path per line.
Largest file to analyze, Deepest folder level, Most files to readSafety limits for huge projects.
Treat .env files as sensitiveReport secrets in .env files and hide their values.
Architecture rules fileSee architecture rules.
Extra vulnerability rules fileA rule pack of your own, added to the built-in checks. Write and edit it with Analyze > Security Rule Editor... (see Writing your own security rules).

After changing a scan setting, click Rescan now in the window, or use File > Rescan (Ctrl+R).

Files and editor

  • Editor for "Open in Editor" - the program that opens source files. Use {file} and {line} where they belong, for example code --goto "{file}:{line}". Leave empty to use your system's default program. Browse… helps you pick it.
  • Folder for downloaded repositories - where File > Open Git Repository suggests putting copies.
  • Download only the latest version by default - the starting state of the Shallow clone box in that window.

Binary Workbench

  • Shortest text to list as a string (3 to 64) and Most strings to show. Debugging always asks before it runs a program; that confirmation cannot be turned off.

Security data

  • Advisory database address - where the Supply Chain view looks up known vulnerabilities. Empty means the public OSV service. Only package names and versions are sent, never your code.
  • Keep advisory answers for - how long a lookup is reused.

AI assistant (optional)

Off by default. When you turn it on, the buttons Explain Node, Explain Finding and Summarize send text from your project (selected code, finding text, summaries) to the server address you enter, which should be a local model server such as http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/generate, with the model name you enter. Only point it at a server you trust with that code. With the assistant off, nothing is sent anywhere. The same page has a block with a one-click Beam preset, Ollama install, sign-in and a connection test; see Local AI assistant and Beam.

Updates

  • Check for updates - Ask me, Automatically or Never. A check only asks the update server for the latest version number.
  • Update channel - stable or beta.
  • Custom update server - only for organizations that host their own updates. Updates are accepted only if signed with a key you have installed.
  • Check for updates now and Stop skipping that version buttons.

Plug-ins and extensions

Shows where plug-ins and extensions are installed and opens their management windows. See Advanced tools.

Data and privacy

Everything the application keeps is stored in one folder on your computer (below). There is no account, and no usage data is sent anywhere. The only network use is what you ask for: opening a repository, vulnerability lookups, the optional AI assistant and update checks.

This page also has buttons to open the data folder, clear the analysis cache (it deletes cached scan results only), clear the recent projects list, restore all suppressed findings, save a copy of my settings to a file and load settings from a file (useful for moving to another computer).

The "Settings & scan options" panel

In the right-hand Element Inspector, Settings & scan options repeats a few options (editor command, scan concurrency, semantic analysis, architecture policy path and extra roots) plus the Git comparison boxes. Edits there are saved immediately and show up in the Settings window too.

Where settings are stored

Settings are saved as settings.json in the application-data folder for your user:

  • Windows: %APPDATA%\Proxalume\settings.json
  • Linux: ~/.config/Proxalume/settings.json

You do not need to edit this file; use the Settings window. A file from an older version keeps working: settings it does not mention take their defaults, and values that are out of range or unsafe (for example an update server that is not https) are corrected when it is read. Load settings from a file never takes the editor command, update settings, advisory address or AI assistant from the file; set those by hand.

Other actions on the Edit menu

  • Clear Analysis Cache deletes the cached results of previous scans so the next scan re-analyzes everything. It does not delete snapshots, suppressions or any of your files.

If a setting does not take effect

See Troubleshooting.

Local AI assistant and Beam (optional)

The AI assistant is an optional helper that can explain a selected graph node, explain a finding, or summarize the repository in plain language. It is off by default, and the rest of Proxalume never needs it.

It works by sending a short text request to an Ollama server that you choose. Ollama is a free program that runs AI models on your computer, and can also pass requests to models it hosts in the cloud. Beam (beam:cloud) is such a cloud model served through Ollama.

Where your text goes

Important A model whose name ends in :cloud, including Beam, runs on Ollama's servers. When you click Explain Node, Explain Finding or Summarize, the text of the selected code, the finding, or the summary is sent over the internet. Nothing is sent until you click one of those buttons, and secret-looking values are removed first on a best-effort basis, but do not use a cloud model on code you are not allowed to share.
SetupWhere requests go
A normal local model, for example llama3Only to Ollama on this computer. Nothing leaves it
Beam or another :cloud modelThrough local Ollama to Ollama's cloud
A different server addressTo that server. Only enter servers you trust

Beam is described by the project owner as free with no usage limit. Its availability and terms are controlled by Ollama and can change; this guide cannot promise them.

One-click setup (Windows)

Open Edit > Settings and find the section AI assistant: Ollama and Beam (optional). A blue hint box there repeats the short version of these steps.

  1. Click Check status. It tells you whether Ollama is installed and running.
  2. If Ollama is missing, click Install Ollama…. A confirmation explains what will happen: the official installer script from https://ollama.com/install.ps1 is downloaded and run in a visible PowerShell window so you can read it. When that window closes, the status refreshes by itself.
  3. Click Sign in to Ollama…. A terminal opens running ollama signin; follow its steps. Cloud models such as Beam need an Ollama account.
  4. Click Use Beam (free, cloud). After you confirm the privacy notice, the address (http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/generate) and model (beam:cloud) are filled in and the assistant is switched on.
  5. That is all: the Settings window saves each change as you make it.
  6. Click Test connection. A tiny request is sent, and the result is shown in plain words.

Then select a node or a finding and use the AI buttons in the right-hand panel (AI assistant (optional, local), or AI Explain on the graph).

Note The buttons only start things after you click them, and installers and sign-in always run in a window you can see. Nothing is installed in the background.

Manual setup, or macOS and Linux

The install and coding-session buttons are Windows-only. Elsewhere:

  1. Install Ollama from https://ollama.com/download.
  2. In a terminal run ollama signin (needed for cloud models).
  3. In Edit > Settings tick Enable optional AI assistant, set the endpoint to http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/generate and the model to beam:cloud, then Apply and Save.
  4. Press Test connection.

To use a local model instead, run for example ollama pull llama3, set the model to llama3, and test.

ollama signin
ollama pull llama3

Beam coding session (separate tool)

Open Beam coding session… opens a terminal in your current project folder and runs:

ollama launch claude --model beam:cloud
Warning This starts a separate coding assistant in that terminal. Unlike the Explain buttons, it can read and change files in the project folder. It is not part of Proxalume's analysis, and its output is not checked by this application. Use it on a copy or a Git branch you can undo.

Troubleshooting

What the test saysWhat to do
"Could not reach the AI server"Ollama is not running. Start it (the Ollama app, or ollama serve), then press Check status
"does not have the model" (404)The model name is wrong or not available. For Beam use exactly beam:cloud; for local models run ollama pull NAME
"refused the request" (401 or 403)Sign in: Sign in to Ollama…, then test again
"rate limiting" (429)Wait and retry
"did not answer in time"Cloud models can be slow to start; try again. Requests time out after two minutes
"Ollama program: not found" after installingClose and reopen Proxalume so it sees the new program, then Check status
"A cloud model needs the local Ollama address"Keep the endpoint at http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/generate; Ollama itself forwards cloud models

If the AI buttons report a failure, the message in the AI panel uses the same wording. When you report a problem, include that message and the output of Check status, but never your Ollama account details.

What it cannot do

  • It does not make findings more certain. Treat AI text as a hint to check, not a verdict; the assistant can be wrong.
  • It does not run code or change your project. (Only the separate coding session can.)
  • It has no usage meter. Limits, if any, come from Ollama.

Related: Settings, Findings, Troubleshooting.

Review before you share

Exports describe your project and can contain sensitive information:

  • File paths and project names (which may include user or customer names).
  • Source snippets in finding evidence and in the graph.
  • Secrets: a finding about a hard-coded credential may quote part of it. The application hides many secrets in exports but cannot promise to catch every one.
  • Binary reports contain strings pulled from the file.

Open the file and search it for tokens, passwords, internal host names and personal data before sending it. Remove or redact them, or share a smaller export (for example SARIF without the graph).

Warning The exports folder lives inside your project. If the project is a Git repository, add exports/ to its .gitignore so you do not commit reports by accident.

If an export fails

See Troubleshooting.

Help

Troubleshooting and FAQ

For every problem: recognize it, try the safe steps, and collect the details listed at the end if you need to report it. None of the steps below asks you to delete your project or reset the whole application.

The application will not launch

  • You see: nothing happens, or a window flashes and closes.
  • Try: make sure you extracted the whole package (do not run it from inside a zip file) and that your operating system is 64-bit. On Windows, SmartScreen may warn about a program from an unknown publisher; only continue if you downloaded the package from the place the developer gave you. On Linux, make the files executable (chmod +x Proxalume Proxalume_Data/Application/Proxalume.App) and run it from a desktop session.
  • Check the package: run Proxalume.exe --selfcheck (Windows) or ./Proxalume --selfcheck (Linux) in a terminal. It prints a line starting selfcheck OK and exits with code 0 when everything works; otherwise it lists what failed.

A project cannot be opened

  • You see: nothing happens after choosing a folder, or a message about the path.
  • Try: confirm the folder exists and you can read it; choose the folder itself, not a single file; avoid network drives and very long paths; check the status bar message. Paths outside the opened project are deliberately blocked for file actions.

A GitHub clone fails

  • You see: a red message in the Open Git Repository window.
  • "Git is not installed": install Git from https://git-scm.com/downloads, restart the application, and try again.
  • "does not exist, is private, or needs sign-in": GitHub gives the same answer for a wrong address and for a private repository. Check the address in a browser. For a private repository, sign in outside this application (Git Credential Manager, gh auth login, or an SSH key) and try again.
  • "The network request failed": check your internet connection, proxy and firewall; the message includes Git's first line of detail.
  • "branch, tag or commit was not found": it was deleted, misspelled, or (in a shallow clone) not downloaded. Use Load branches and tags, or untick Shallow clone.
  • "destination folder already exists and is not empty": choose a new folder. Nothing was changed.
  • "not enough free disk space": free some space or choose another drive.
  • Cancelled or failed clones remove only what they created; a folder that existed before is left alone.

Never paste a token into the address or a bug report. See Opening a Git repository.

Authentication is unavailable

There is no sign-in screen in the application, by design. GitHub access for private repositories uses the credentials you set up for Git itself (Git Credential Manager, GitHub CLI, or an SSH key), so check them in a terminal first (git ls-remote https://github.com/owner/repository). The optional AI assistant has its own, separate setup; see Local AI assistant.

A language or file format is unsupported

  • You see: files counted as Unsupported on Project Health, or an empty graph for part of the project.
  • Try: check the supported languages. A file type without an analyzer cannot be added from inside the application. Use the file explorer to read it.

Analysis is incomplete

  • You see: Analyzed is much smaller than Discovered, or tiles for skipped, partial or failed files.
  • Try: check Excluded Directories; raise Max file size or Max directory depth in Settings if large or deep files were skipped; turn semantic analysis on; then Rescan. Remember that dynamically built code cannot be analyzed statically.

A parser reports an error

  • You see: a finding that names a file and line with a parse or read error.
  • Try: open the file at that line (Open in Editor) and look for a syntax problem or a very new language feature. Other files are not affected; the failure is isolated.

Graph results appear incomplete

Dashed lines are guesses; missing lines may be relationships the analyzer cannot see (dynamic calls, reflection, other services). Clear the filter (Reset Filters), check that the file was analyzed, and see if you isolated a node. Use Fit to View to make sure the picture is not simply off screen.

A binary cannot be disassembled

  • You see: "unsupported architecture", zero functions, or obvious nonsense instructions.
  • Try: check what is supported. For a firmware image, open it again with Open Raw / Firmware Image… and the correct architecture and base address. Packed or encrypted files (entropy near 8 in Triage) must be unpacked first; the application does not unpack.

A file changes while it is being inspected

The Workbench reads the file once when you open it. If another program changes it, what you see is the old copy. Patches and hex saves check the file on disk first and are refused when it no longer matches ("the file changed on disk"). Re-open the file and repeat your edit.

A cache or workspace cannot be loaded

If results look stale, use Edit > Clear Analysis Cache and then Rescan. This only removes cached analysis results, not snapshots, suppressions, annotations or your files. A corrupt annotation or settings file is ignored and replaced by defaults instead of crashing the application.

An export fails

Make sure the project folder is writable and not full, that the file is not open in another program, and that the path is not too long. Exports go to an exports folder inside the project; a read-only project (such as a network share or a zip) cannot receive them. Binary reports let you pick a different location.

Analysis runs slowly

Open a smaller folder, add custom exclusions for generated code and large data, lower Max file size, switch off semantic analysis, and use Max concurrency that suits your processor. In the 3D City, lower the LOD Nodes slider. The first scan is slowest; later scans reuse cached results for unchanged files.

An optional dependency or external tool is unavailable

Git comparison needs git on your PATH. The deepest Java and Python analysis may need those runtimes; without them the analyzers use simpler methods and mark files as partly analyzed. The AI assistant needs the local model server you configured. Everything else works without extra tools.

A setting does not take effect

Scan settings apply to the next scan: click Rescan now in the Settings window, or use File > Rescan. Everything else in the Settings window is saved and applied as soon as you change it (a text box applies when you press Enter or click elsewhere); a red message under a box means the value was refused and not saved. If a value looks wrong after saving, reopen Settings to confirm it, and check that numbers are within range (for example concurrency 1–64).

The documentation window will not open or a page is blank

The guide is built into the application. If the Documentation window reports that the guide could not be loaded, the installation is incomplete: extract the package again. A single damaged page shows a notice and the rest still works. You can keep working in the main window while the guide is open.

What to include in a bug report

  • The application version (Help > About) and your operating system.
  • What you did, what you expected and what happened.
  • The text of any message, and the status-bar text.
  • The output of Proxalume.exe --selfcheck (Windows) or ./Proxalume --selfcheck (Linux).
  • The kind and rough size of the project or file (not its contents), and the settings you changed.

Do not include access tokens, passwords, private source code or unredacted exports.

Glossary

Plain-language definitions of terms used in the application and in this guide. A term marked (concept only) is explained for background; the application has no feature for it.

A-C

Advisory. A published report of a known vulnerability in a package, with the versions it affects. The application looks them up in the OSV database.

Analyzer. A component that understands one language or file type and extracts symbols and relationships from it.

API contract. (concept only) A formal description of what a web service accepts and returns (for example an OpenAPI file). The application does not compare contracts.

Architectural policy. A set of rules about which kinds of components may depend on which others. See architecture rules.

Basic block. A straight run of instructions with one entry and one exit. The boxes in a control-flow graph.

Binary. A compiled program or library file, such as a Windows .exe, as opposed to source code.

Call graph. A map of which functions call which others.

CodeGraph. The application's model of a project: all its nodes and edges. What the 2D graph draws.

Control-flow graph (CFG). A diagram of one function's basic blocks and the jumps between them.

Cross-reference (xref). A link from one place to another that uses it, such as a call site and the function it calls, or a string and the code that reads it.

Cyclomatic complexity. A count of the decision points in a function. Higher means more paths to understand and test.

D-F

Decompiled code. Source-like code reconstructed from a binary. The application does not decompile; it disassembles.

Dependency. Something one part of a program relies on: another file, class, library or service.

Digital signature. (concept only) A cryptographic proof that a file came from a particular key holder and was not altered. The application does not verify signatures.

Disassembly. Machine instructions shown as readable text such as mov eax, 1.

Edge. A line in the graph; a relationship between two nodes.

Entropy. A measure of how random a file's bytes are (0 to 8 bits per byte). High values suggest compressed or encrypted data.

Evidence (of a relationship). How the relationship was found: declared, resolved, inferred, potential or unresolved. See evidence kinds.

File offset. A position counted from the start of a file on disk.

Finding. A possible problem reported by a rule. Not a confirmed vulnerability.

Function. A named, reusable piece of code. In binaries the application discovers functions even when the file has no names.

Fuzzing. (concept only) Testing by feeding a program large amounts of unexpected input to find crashes. The application does not fuzz.

H-R

Lockfile. A file written by a package manager that records the exact version of every package installed, such as package-lock.json or composer.lock.

Hash. A fingerprint of a file's bytes (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256 are shown in the Workbench). Equal hashes mean identical contents.

Heuristic. A rule of thumb that is usually right but can be wrong. Results based on heuristics are shown as potential or inferred.

Package URL (purl). A standard text identifier for a package, such as pkg:npm/lodash@4.17.21.

Node. A box in the graph: a file, class, function, route, table and so on.

Provenance. (concept only) A verifiable record of where and how an artifact was built from source. The application does not check provenance.

Raw image. A file with no header describing it, such as firmware; you tell the application its architecture and base address.

RVA / virtual address. A location in memory as the program sees it once loaded. An RVA is measured from the image base.

Rescan. Analyze the project again, reusing cached results for unchanged files.

S-Z

SARIF. A standard file format for static-analysis results, readable by many code-scanning tools.

SBOM (software bill of materials). A standard list of the components and versions a piece of software contains. The Supply Chain view exports a CycloneDX SBOM and compares an imported one. See Supply chain.

Shallow clone. A copy of a repository that has only the latest snapshot of its files, not its full history.

Snapshot. A saved analysis result used as a baseline for comparison.

Suppression. Hiding a finding you reviewed. It does not change source code.

Symbol. A named thing in code: a class, function, variable, route, table.

Test coverage. (concept only) How much of the code a test suite runs. Not the same as analysis coverage, which is how much of a project this application could read.

Runtime trace. (concept only) A recording of what a program actually did while running. The application analyzes files statically and records no runtime data.

Static analysis. Examining code without running it.

Known gaps in this guide and planned features

Gaps in this guide

  • Screenshots cover the main window, the 2D graph, the Binary Workbench, the control-flow graph and Settings. The Supply Chain view and the GitHub window are described in text only.
  • Private-repository access uses your own Git sign-in and includes sign-in, proxy, TLS and SSH diagnostics in the Open Git Repository window across GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps and self-hosted Git servers; live network cloning still depends on your system Git configuration.
  • The guide was written by checking each page against the application's menus and controls; some behaviors (for example exact wording of status messages) may differ slightly between releases.
  • The guide covers the Windows and Linux packages. A macOS package is not provided, so macOS-specific instructions are not included.
  • Language-specific analysis details (for example exactly which Laravel constructs are recognized) are summarized, not exhaustive.
  • A single-file copy of this guide, which opens in any web browser and can be printed, ships with the application in its Documentation folder.

Features that are not available (so are not described as steps)

These are not part of the application today. This page lists them so you do not search for them.

Source analysis: downloading submodules or LFS files automatically without being asked, and submodules that use SSH; saving credentials; online transparency-log queries for build provenance (existing AFL++, libFuzzer and Go fuzzing runs can be imported as read-only evidence, and user-selected fuzz harnesses can be run in a bounded working directory with execution timeouts on explicit confirmation).

Binary Workbench: pseudo-code for unrecognized computed jumps in 32-bit ARM, RISC-V, PowerPC and MIPS, and for 64-bit PowerPC and MIPS; masked EVEX opmasks and cross-lane vector shuffles in pseudo-code (128-bit SSE/SSE2, 128/256/512-bit AVX/AVX2/AVX-512/FMA3 and 64-bit/128-bit AArch64 NEON packed arithmetic, compares, broadcasts and shifts are translated, as are 32-bit and 64-bit pointer, array, structure-array and PDB/user structure layouts); plug-ins that can change the binary or use files and the network (plug-ins are read-only and sandboxed by design); a hosted internet server for shared annotations (notes can be exported/imported or synchronized live across a shared folder); assembly macros; unpacking legacy compressed RAR 1.5–2.9 streams, NSIS 2 installers, multi-volume encrypted InstallShield setups and Quantum-compressed cabinets (ZIP, TAR, GZIP, Zstandard, 7z, RAR 5, stored RAR 4 entries, CAB, MSI, NSIS 3, Inno Setup 6.5+, WiX Burn bundles and single-volume InstallShield cabinets are supported).

Where a related partial feature exists it is described on the page for that topic, with its limits.

Reporting a documentation problem

If an instruction does not match what you see, note the guide page title, the step and the application version (Help > About), and include them in your report (see Troubleshooting).

Limitations

These are things the application does not do, so you do not look for them. The topic Known gaps in the User Guide has the current list; in summary:

  • Source analysis: automatic unprompted download of Git submodules or LFS objects, SSH submodules, saving Git credentials inside the application, and online transparency-log queries for build provenance.
  • Binary Workbench: pseudo-code for 64-bit PowerPC and 64-bit MIPS, or masked EVEX opmasks and cross-lane vector shuffles; debugging macOS programs, ARM targets or shared libraries; assembly macros; and unpacking password-protected 7z/RAR archives, legacy compressed RAR 1.5–2.9 streams, NSIS 2 installers, multi-volume encrypted InstallShield setups or Quantum-compressed cabinets.
  • Forensic cases: live volatile memory capture from a running system, full Windows kernel memory dumps and multi-gigabyte raw or E01 disk images (interactive case acquisition caps individual files at 50 MB).
  • Plug-ins and collaboration: WebAssembly plug-ins run inside a deterministic read-only sandbox and cannot modify binaries, read other files or use the network; shared binary notes synchronize via exported files or a shared folder rather than a hosted internet server.
  • Licensing and CLI: unattended licensed command-line sessions in headless environments (interactive license activation is required per installation).

Results are aids, not guarantees. Static analysis cannot see code that is built or loaded dynamically at run time, and findings require human review.
